segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Yes, sir, Mr. Chairman, honorable members of Tampa City Council. It is indeed my pleasure to be with you and stand next to one of the best --

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Charlie Miranda. I want to get sworn in before I speak later on with the rays. I want to make sure I tell the truth. There was a movie about you called to tell the truth, your honor. Anyway, the convention that we have in the City Of Tampa, the businesses that we have in the City Of Tampa, the convention center, it's all related to various many things. One of them is the Florida Tampa Aquarium. Let me say this. I remember when mayor Sandy Freedman thought about the idea and took it to the task of having it built. And it was open, what, march of 1995. It's an honor because when I was first elected in '74, what's there, where the convention center is at, what about 80 feet of citrus nitrate and open air. It was a little different. Now that convention center has made -- i'm not going to brag about it because I didn't do it, but roger and his staff did it -- four years of over 1 million people in attendance of the Florida Tampa Convention Center. Roger is the one responsible for it along with his staff. He'll talk about that later. But the Tampa City Council proudly recognizes the Florida aquarium for being voted one of the ten best aquariums in the country in USA today. That is a deep honor and goes to you and your staff. And these things happen, global leader in maritime conservation, aquarium hosted the world's first center for special survival focus on coral conservation, pioneering and reproduction of the atlantic and cactus corals. I don't know too much about cactus corals. Tampa City Council present the commendation to the Florida aquarium on the 27th day of August, 2026, outstanding contribution to downtown Tampa, continued dedication to a stronger, more vibrant community, healthier future for the Tampa Bay region. All together this means a whole, whole, whole lot to the city because it brings what it calls tourist dollars. One of the reasons that Tampa is doing what they are doing. Not only do they do that, but the children that go there learn a lot about conservation and what to do with an aquarium. Thank you, City Council members. On behalf of our board --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: You have to say your name. Sorry about that. I will say again thank you to Councilman Miranda. Thank you, council members, for the commendation for your Florida aquarium as we like to say as well. As the councilman mentioned, we opened in 1995. You know our story. Over the last few years, we have said make no little plans at the Florida aquarium. We have been driving to create an experience and an aquarium that you and our community not only are proud of, but deserves in a world-class aquarium. This is a great honor. So on behalf of myself, our board of directors, our 300 members of our staff, including tony and Sally, who are here. Thank you very much for the honor and we'll Continue To Drive to make an impact and make this aquarium the best aquarium in the world. Again, one you and our community are very proud of. Thank you very much. [ applause ]

segments.text: I just want to say congratulations. The Aquarium is a real asset to our community. One of my favorite things about the Aquarium is if you did not know, you can go to the Public Library and you can check out tickets to the Aquarium. I think you can get four at a time.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: You could take your whole family and don't have to pay for it. You're checking it out from the library. It is amazing, phenomenal program along with many of the programs they do. It is a wonderful asset. I really appreciate what you're doing. Your renovation plans are going to help make it even better.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, roger. Thank you for doing everything that you've done with the aquarium. I'm really looking forward to the expansion plans and new exhibits that you are bringing to the community and to the kids and be able to learn about wildlife from all over the world. It is as Councilwoman Hurtak said, a great asset. As Councilman Miranda said, it really is remarkable, especially when we're talking about these types of things. You had an area that was dilapidated warehouses, nefarious kind of businesses and no economic activity, the government got involved and built the aquarium. It changed Tampa forever. We have billions and billions of dollars now of growth and infrastructure and these beautiful areas. I don't know if we would have the streetcar, channelside, Water Street, now future of Gasworx and the revival of Ybor City without the aquarium. Anchor piece. I don't know if amalie arena would be there without the aquarium. It's remarkable that one small project becomes a catalyst. We're even going to have a ferris wheel. It is remarkable, and it is a beautiful building. My family, my son, my daughter-in-law, and my granddaughter are members and are there frequently. I think my granddaughter is only 6, but she can name every animal and fish in that building. Thank you for everything you do. Thank you for your staff. You have a wonderful staff. Great experience. As Councilwoman Hurtak said, if you haven't gone to the aquarium, go to the Florida aquarium.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: I wanted to, one, when you and I met with -- along with tony, and you have such a vision for what you want to do with the aquarium. I'm really excited to see the expansion as well. I'm just happy to have this asset in the community but also thank you both for your leadership and your outreach and making sure all of our youth are being exposed and our community can be exposed and come and enjoy the aquarium. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. Have a beautiful day.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: All righty. Good morning, council. Councilwoman Naya Young. I am very excited today because we are presenting a commendation to Mr. Jamal Jefferson who is the Tampa Bay Buccaneers inspired change, change maker award. Tampa City Council proudly honors Mr. Jamal Jefferson for his role as a pivotal community leader and mentor in the Tampa Bay community. This commendation is in recognition of Mr. Jefferson's dedication to uplifting the youth of our community through his leadership as site supervisor at the Jackson Heights Nfl Yet Center since 2010. The Nfl Yet Center as we all know is a staple in the East Tampa community and provides a safe space for our children daily. Provide after-school programs, summer programming, sports mentorship and in partnership with the buccaneers, the guitar, ukulele lessons, illustrate the variety of paths and opportunities available for students at the Nfl Yet Center. Mr. Jefferson, supervisors the teens leading change program with Tampa parks and rec and helped to organize the prime-time turf takeover earlier this year to support teens wishing for more positive gathering spaces. Through his work, Mr. Jefferson demonstrated an unwavering commitment to providing a safe haven for children and teens in Tampa. He has been a true leader, public servant and someone that our youth look up to. In gratitude to his efforts, Tampa City Council presents this commendation on this 27th day of August, 2026, to Mr. Jamal Jefferson as Tampa Bay Buccaneers inspired change, change maker award recipient. [ applause ] I see the cameras and everything. [ laughter ] happy to know they came to see me this morning. All sincerity, thank you to Tampa City Council. Thank you, Councilwoman Young, and your office for the recognition also. Thank you to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The buccaneers have always been a great supportive partner in parks and rec and Jackson Heights Nfl Yet Center. I would be remiss if I didn't thank my wife who graciously shares me with the community all the time. My mom is here this morning. [ applause ] my mom is here this morning, my brother, my family. Some of my colleagues and peers and other community partners are here this morning. I can't leave without thanking the staff at Jackson Heights. Shalanda, ralph, martin, o'mara. I'm the person that people see all the time. I'm the face of the yet center, but they really do the work. They are the boots on the ground. The ones engaging every day. I won't hold up too much time because I heard you have something big to do today. I'll get out of the way. Thank you all for the recognition. Thank the community for the support, and we appreciate it so much. [ applause ]

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Thank you, mr. Chairman. Martin Shelby, City Council attorney. Briefly, the rules of decorum for today's meeting, and as the chair has stated, members of the public are allowed a reasonable opportunity at the beginning of today's meeting to address any item on the agenda before the City Council takes official action on the item. As he stated, per council's rules, preference will be given to those speaking on agenda items. Three minute time limit applies to all speakers providing public comment. Speakers and members of the public are also reminded to please refrain from disruptive behavior, including making vulgar or threatening remarks or making or causing disruptive noises or sounds or displaying signs or graphics. Please direct your comments to the entire City Council rather than individual members. The chair Will rule out of order any person who speaks without being recognized or attempts to address the City Council from outside the speaker area at the lectern. Persons failing to comply with council's rules may also be ruled out of order and at the discretion of the chair may be removed from the chambers and old city hall for the remainder of today's meeting. Again, if you are here to speak on items set for public hearing and items 59 to 70 and 71 through 76 you will have that opportunity. Also, no public comment will be taken later during staff reports. The time to speak to those items and items on the consent agenda is now during agenda public comment. Finally, please, City Council, refrain from engaging a speaker under public comment. The public should be aware that the City Council does not take questions or have a dialogue during general public comment. This is your opportunity to express your position to the Tampa City Council. Thank you.

segments.text: Since we have a lot of new people, I want to remind folks, again, this is one-way communication during public comment. segments.text: Thank you, pam. James Ransom followed by Stephanie Poynor. I first want to let you know that i'm standing here with some board members from Toba Leadership Institute to thank you all for listening to our concerns, reading our concerns about agenda number 59. It has to do with the EBO ordinance proposed change, which we asked you most recently to set aside indefinitely. The reason for that is because we know that taxpayers and voters who look like us and anyone else in the room should feel valued and have a real opportunity to actually do business with the City Of Tampa. Anything that takes us further away from that certainly codifying a law change is going to make it a little more challenging to fix that later. We provided to the city attorney, to City Council, and the mayor further alternatives to look at, rather than change the law, look at policies that might still achieve not breaking the law, but still valuing the taxpayers and citizens who look like everyone that should be able to have a fair opportunity to actually do work with the City Of Tampa. So i'm here to thank you for that. Council Member Hurtak really pointed that out and helped to support us initially and Council Member Carlson and all of you, all of you agreed to sort of slow it down. Let the attorneys go back and look at it. Attorneys sent us very voluminous legal jargon. We sent back very voluminous legal responses. They should take some time to look at what we sent back and then suspend and set aside, we think indefinitely, that situation, rather than change the law. That's why we came this morning, speak about this particular issue and we'll talk about other things later on in the agenda.

Every year I analyze the top three salaries in each and every department in the city. And the proposal that the mayor brought forward, she said that there was $24.5 Million in salary increases. Chief Bennett told me about 80% of that is union increases. Now, I don't know about you, but if I were in the union, I would be able to say, yes, it's okay to postpone the raises until after November the 5th because we may cut our budget significantly. And we need to rethink this. The union needs to rethink this. Everybody on staff needs to rethink this. I'm not saying take away their money. I'm saying let's just hold off on the increases. But I just analyzed a couple of departments because they were the ones that threw up at me. Marketing and Communications up by 25%. The director sent an e-mail to you guys and said, no, that's wrong. It's actually correct. His department acquired three more people. I guess he has a hard time going from 9 to 12. That's a lot of math. Bottom line is, his department did grow by 25% monetarily. The next one, and this is funny because this came up on my timeline on facebook. The mayor's office. This picture is from a meeting in 2024. Two years ago, I talked about the mayor's salary and her department. This is five people. Their increase will be $166,000 this year for those -- i'm sorry. That's between 2023 budget and this budget coming up. 167,000. One person in her department will be getting a 21.9% Raise. That's ridiculous. It's absolutely absurd. We have to look at all these. No one wants to lose their jobs. That's reality. We have no idea what's going to happen. But looking at these two departments, it shows us that we're not being conservative enough with this budget. The other thing I want to talk about for just a minute is item number 41. I want to know when the policy for the City Of Tampa -- when the City Of Tampa's policy changed that somebody can come back and work for the city less than two years after they resigned, after they left the city. Vik Bhide's name on there not once but twice. He approved the contract when he worked for the city. Now we approve contracts and then come back to work for the contract? Yeah, we really probably need to look into number 41 a little bit deeper. Because I have lots and lots of great employees who work for the city who are my friends, and they have sat on the sidelines for the last two years and haven't been able to advocate and do work for the city. But this guy can?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Mr. Fernandez defers. We've got Sandra Tyrell. Alison date, and Mr. Hayes. Good morning. Alison date, followed by Mr. Hayes and Valerie Bullock. Go ahead. Start with your name, please. You'll have three minutes. My name is Sandra Atiles-Tyrrell. I am a co-owner of a local small business founded in 2018. Long before it existed I had the privilege of serving the City Of Tampa as sales representative for large national distributor. Beginning in 2007 I work directly with the City departments, learn how they operate, became familiar with their needs and developed relationships built on responsiveness, reliability and trust. That experience gave me the invaluable knowledge and tools to understand government procurement. When my husband kevin and I built it from the ground up, we still needed the opportunity to demonstrate what our company could do. The City Of Tampa shelter market program gave us that opportunity. This program is not a hand-out. It does not guarantee us a contract or guarantee our success. It allows qualified small businesses to compete with a smaller pool where capabilities can be seen and fairly evaluated. We must still understand the specifications, submit competitive pricing, deliver and address challenges. The program may open the door but the performance determines whether we earn the city's trust to serve again. Although it is a small business, we have built strong partnerships with manufacturers, distributors, and technical experts. This relationship expands our capabilities and help us locate difficult products, obtain technical support and provide competitive solutions and respond with the personal attention and flexibility that a small business can offer. Through the shelter market program, we have gained valuable knowledge, established strong performance history and grown into one of the city's trusted suppliers. For that, kevin and I are profoundly grateful. Because of this experience, I regularly speak about this program with other small business owners. Through my involvement with the Tampa Bay Latin Chamber and other community organizations, I encourage entrepreneurs to become certified, understand the city's procurement process and pursue opportunities. I share story because I want other capable small businesses to know that this resource exist and that success is possible. When one local business gains access, performs well and then helps another business Find Its Way to the table, the impact reaches far beyond one contract or company. The shelter market program did not build our success. It gave us a fair opportunity to build it ourselves. Whatever name or structure the program carries moving forward, I respectfully ask that you strengthen the shelter market at ITs heart. Thank you so very much for letting us share our story.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. After more advice and counsel from our City Council attorney, it was brought to my attention that the hearing, even though it is a hearing and normally you would speak during the hearing, because it is a non-quasi-judicial hearing, it would be basically no harm to the record to allow. The question that we need to be concerned with today, the controlling question is, what will Tampa look like in the 21st century? This ordinance has two-part disparity. The first one is race disparity, and the second is economic disparity. So I want to talk about the economic disparity because the numbers that are living in 2026 are from 2008. The dollar has eroded the buying power. Currently, every dollar that we put down is for 63 cents. And the 2.5 Mill threshold that we currently have for construction has eroded by approximately 35% and is worth 1.6 Mill in today's dollars. The African American wealth is at risk right now by 2053 it is deemed to be at zero. By 2045, this will be a minority nation. One thing I can definitely speak directly to as a part of the ordinance is the professional services shelter market threshold. Because of that threshold, I was able to gain business from them as well who successfully needed that program, not only to win bids in this area, but to be in compliance. And I was happy to service them. And to keep it short, I respectfully urge you to approve the ordinance. Because of this, it's very helpful to us as small businesses to be recognized in more than one area. It's practical, overdue update that helps small local businesses like mine compete fairly and grow. Thank you for your time and your investment in Tampa's small business community. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Judy. Tommy Whitehead followed by Michael Grant followed by David Sinclair. Thank you for letting me speak today. My name is Tommy Whitehead. With Tomko Solutions, local conglomerate of companies, construction, a.i., Media. Recently named ink 5,000. Local boy. My office overlooks your office. This kind of thing is important to me. I've had the privilege of serving on the equal business opportunity committee for the last year. To those that oppose this revision on principle, they are right. The disparity is real. It's documented. I share the concern. I'm married to a Black man. I have personally seen discriminatory actions in the last several years against him and we've been together more than a decade. Still exists. I wish it didn't. Look at what the program is delivering right now. Everything comes from the city's public records on the website. Anybody in this room can pull it. I'm surprise nobody has quoted the numbers yet. Let's talk about the program. 64 solicitations from May 2025 through June 2026. Roughly $2 million in awarded value. The city received 504 bids. Certified firms accounted for 11 of them. Let's break this down into a couple of categories. Black-Owned businesses. 226 certified businesses. There is one firm out of 504 bids. One firm that even pursued anything. So we have an amazing organization, toba is great. I love what they do, but there is a misunderstanding. I'm only quoting numbers, not a motion. One participant. Hispanic firm, 290 certified, three firms that bid. One of them actually won. Zero women owned certified businesses bid during this period. So one win, 159,000 out of $2 million, about 7, 8 percent from certified firms. I'm going to ask the committee here, I agree with the idea that we should accept diversity and pick up disparity, but there is nothing you can do by keeping this ordinance that changes these numbers. They haven't applied when they had the availability to apply. I say they, I say any diversity owned business or small owned business. So why are we holding up something or considering posting back something that they haven't even worked for? A single Black-Owned firm that didn't -- the single Black-Owned firm that did bid didn't lose on bias. It's numbers. The bid was 283,000 for a job awarded for $147,000. I encourage the committee to actually look at the numbers and realize that right now all these small owned businesses, all the diversity owned businesses are small owned businesses. They benefit from increased shelters, especially construction companies where construction costs have skyrocketed and we can't bid any more at the values because of the shelter caps and small business purchases and procurement card purchases actually increase the threshold to allow the smaller businesses without going through the bid process.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Michael Grant followed by David Sinclair, followed by Alyssa White. Good morning, michael. Start with your name. You'll have three minutes. Michael Grant. The boundless group. We currently do work for the city. We're here in support of the ordinance change. I'm not a local boy. I'm a naturalized citizen from another country that has no opportunities. The city has given us opportunity to grow in a small business. But there is a lot of work to do. We don't want to sugarcoat anything. Accepting this ordinance is only one step in keeping the program alive and changing. The items that are addressed in the ordinance is addressing reality currently, right? Increasing the threshold, increasing the numbers, allowing small businesses to bid and be competitive. I definitely want to call out toba as some of their insights in what they shared valid. But I do also want to request from them as well that let's not stop progress. Let's work together. Let's partner, as we've done currently. One last call-out, I want to say thanks to the committee, the EBO Committee for all the time they spent. I sat in not only half the meetings and I calculated in billable hours we would have lost about $60,000. That's just me. Times that by 12 people. They did it for free. So we need to consider that as well. And then lastly, call out ms. Bertha Mitchell. She is tiny but mighty. She stands up for small businesses. I've seen her do it. I've seen her take the brunt for standing up for small businesses. Want to call her out and say thanks for doing that. We should all support her. That's it. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Appreciate it. David Sinclair followed by Alyssa White followed by Cabela Mueller. Good morning, sir. Start with your name. My name is David Sinclair. I'm a volunteer with the Sierra Club. The city wonderful climate action and equity plan speaks to understanding the needs and concerns of the front line communities. Included in your plan, you speak of having listened to the community, having listened to what the community says that wants to promote clean energy and maintain affordability. Also included in your clean energy plan, you mentioned a nifty contribution from Tampa electric, where Tampa electric says that TECO is the gate-keeper to 100% clean energy and renewable energy. It is a moment now to listen to the community and to step forward and give the opportunity for the community to have a town hall meeting. I invite all of the members of the City Council to an October 22nd opportunity for a town hall meeting in the community. So on October 22, 6:30 p.m. At the barksdale senior center, 1801 North Lincoln Avenue in Tampa, will have an opportunity for town hall meeting, the community can come together. We're inviting officials of Tampa electric to come also so that we can as a community talk about the issues of affordability and clean energy, particularly at a moment when the electric rates of Tampa electric have risen to the third highest in the US. And at times when the energy production of Tampa electric is only 17% in the sunshine state. You are all invited to come October 22 so that we may speak as a community and deal with some of the issues that are very important to us. You are all invited to attend. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, sir, appreciate it. We have four more in-person speakers. I'll call those four names. If you believe you are supposed to speak this morning on these items, please bring your attention to myself so we can fix that issue if there is a problem. Alyssa White, Isabella Mueller, Surgret Doss and Ash Leyva. My name is Alyssa White. I'm the climate justice organizer with Florida Student Power and a member of the Hillsborough Affordable Energy Coalition. I'm here today because I am deeply disappointed in the lack of action from the city on the rising cost of utility bills. Not because the city doesn't recognize that these rising electric costs are hurting people, you do recognize it. I think we've been able to meet with most of you, and you've all agreed that this is a pressing issue for community members, but what is disappointing is we keep hearing that this is a serious issue, yet we are not seeing any action that should come with that acknowledgment. While we are here today discussing a lot of new business, Tampa family members are struggling right now with their electric bills. They are continuing to open their bills and wonder how they are going to pay them. These aren't just abstract numbers on a spreadsheet. These are your constituents, our coalition has been door knocking. We've hosted events, and we've talked to community members about their struggles with their bills and the city hasn't done that. Here is the part that I think deserves even more attention. Tampa taxpayers are paying this bill twice. Residents are paying their own increasingly expensive bills and their tax dollars are also paying for the city's electric bills. According to the city in fiscal year 2025, you all spent approximately $25.1 Million on electricity. And the city did something right. It reduced energy consumption by switching to solar options and you guys saved about 9.3%, Which is about $1.8 Million. And that's great. Even after using substantially less energy, rising rates and the rate hikes are eating at those additional savings. So when the city itself is being financially impacted by these rate increases, I don't understand how we can say that this is simply outside of the city's purview. You may not control the rates, but you're absolutely in control of whether you speak up. You're in control of whether you use your voice, and you are in control on whether this council stands with the people who elected you. Frankly, residents need more than an acknowledgment that this is a problem because we are the ones living with it. We need action. So i'm asking this council to do something concrete. There are options. Pass a resolution. I know that we approached each of you with it, calling for affordable, transparent and reasonable energy rates for Tampa residents and formally communicating that position to the Public Service Commission. Hold a public town hall. I know my colleague david just talked about that, or bring TECO and the appropriate state regulators to the table and make them answer questions from the residents who are paying these bills. If the city believes that there are limits to what they can legally or practically do, please tell us what the limits are and what you are going to do within those limits. Saying we don't control the rates cannot be the end of the conversation. It should be the beginning of a question of what you guys can do. We have already demonstrated that the city can reduce ITs energy --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Your time is up. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Also, if you are downstairs and you are here for a public hearing, if you are downstairs and here for a public hearing, please come to Tampa City Council chambers, please. Isabella Mueller followed by Surgret Doss. It's nice to see all of you. I'm ysabella with food and water watch and Hillsborough Affordable Energy Coalition. I know we have a really packed agenda today. I'm here again to make the ask to pass an affordable energy resolution and to join us in our work for fighting for affordable energy in Hillsborough County and Tampa. As Alyssa mentioned, we've had this conversation with most of you. We all agree that TECO bills are too high and really needs to be something done about this. So earlier this year, we came to you urging you to pass this resolution, calling on our State Lawmakers to pass affordable energy reform, and we did this because we believe that you all can be champions in advocating for affordable energy solutions and standing up for your constituents who are struggling to pay their bills. Since hearing your concerns, I have revised a new resolution for all of you to look at. And this includes specific actions that we all believe are within your purview that you can take action on, such as opposing electricity rate hikes that disproportionately burden residents, urging State Lawmakers to pass affordable energy reform next year, utilizing state and -- funding for energy efficiency and clean energy programs. Requesting the release of Tampa specific shut-off data which would be useful to have. Connecting residents with more cost-saving energy programs. Opposing the construction of hyperscaled data centers and calling for accessible and district hearings. Tampa electric is expected to have another rate case next year. That's something that you all can directly do when that's happening. With that, we've heard your concerns. I drafted a new resolution for you all to review and i'll pass that over after this. However, as Alyssa mentioned, I have been pretty disappointed with my -- or with the lack of response from council members lately. The coalition has been reaching out to your offices all summer, calling, e-mailing, and I know you all are busy, but we have not been getting any response from you. Again, this is something that we feel we can work on and find solutions that are within your purview to help with this issue. I also understand as we have mentioned that you guys do not directly set the rates for Tampa electric. We know that. You do not control the Public Service Commission. Ultimately reform will come from the state level in tallahassee. But we also all know that change does not stop at the top. It stops at the bottom. That's why we're asking to you join us in this work, start at the local level, and really start pushing forward with these small solutions and changes that we can make so that then we Can Ultimately Drive that state-level reform that we're really looking to, to crack down on just the pure corporate greed we're seeing from the Utility Companies. With that, I Hope You look at this new resolution and happy to discuss more over coffee or another meeting.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: If you have a document to share, would you hand -- [indiscernible] Mr. Doss followed by Ashley Levi. Amazing how the time flies. I'm 58. But he gives me hope that the kids that he influences will hopefully take his lead and become better people than, of course, I have. segments.text: Good morning, council. Carl Brody, legal. Development.

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: We want to thank you for the opportunity to discuss the proposed changes to the ordinance formerly the equal business opportunity now strategic business development. I want to talk to you a little bit about what the ordinance does, what the benefits are, and to address some of the concerns that the community has about the impacts of making these changes. As I came to you last time, we did note that this isn't what we want to do. We agree with everybody, diversity is important, but we're stuck with several federal executive orders and directives. We have a state law that just passed and will go into effect in January. Between these and the other interpretations that we're getting from the courts, legally we're being told that we are in jeopardy if we have a -- conscious program. Very importantly, the new law sb 1134 which would be codified, that covers the waterfront. That confers everything. It basically states we can't have any kind of program that provides any special benefit based on race, gender, ethnicity. There is no exception whereas at least with the courts there's some consideration in terms of if we can satisfy a strict scrutiny standard. That's not provided for in the state law.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Point of order. We should have our attorney in here for this. Where is Mr. Shelby? We should have our attorney in here.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Mr. Shelby, return to Council Chambers.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: I apologize.

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: Would you like me to continue?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Pause, please. If staff in the back can find Mr. Shelby and put him back in his box.

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: If I can approach separately, Mr. Whitehead failed to provide support from the South Tampa Chamber of Commerce. If I can provide --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Provide that Mr. Shelby. He is back and you can proceed with the presentation.

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: As noted, state law is Black and White. It's saying that we can't have any programs that provide any benefits based on race, gender, ethnicity. That has to be addressed. How we address this and even previously when we were concerned with the federal changes was that we suspended the current program as it applied to race and gender. Right now, status quo is, none of the businesses that we're concerned about are receiving any of the benefits of the program we Have In Place right now. That's suspended. They are not getting any benefits. What this ordinance does is it addresses both those firms impacted now and other small businesses by increasing the thresholds. What's that mean? That means that if I have a --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Pause for one moment. If your cell phone is not on silent, please silence it now. If it goes off again, i'll ask you to leave the Council Chambers. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: What does that threshold issue mean? That threshold issue means that if I have a business, whether a Black business, Hispanic Business, Small Business, I graduate from the program, which means I can no longer receive the benefits of participating in the sheltered market. When I go to bid, I only go to bid against the really big firms. That will limit my ability to be successful. Increasing that threshold allows these businesses that are successful to continue to receive the benefits of the shelter market and bid against other firms of similar size and not have to bid against the large, large firms. Also, the thresholds are set on our projects. Our projects are set at a level from 2009. So that means we're still 15 years behind in terms of inflation, in terms of costs. We all know how much those have gone up. This is increase the projects that these firms can bid on. All this is of special benefit just for Small Businesses, race conscious so that we avoid any kind of challenges from any party that might decide that they want to challenge any changes to the ordinance that would provide a special benefit based on race or gender. It's very important to understand that what we're doing here is going to benefit all businesses, but especially going to benefit our Small Businesses that have a racial or gender component. Real quick. To address some of toba's points, we're doing that now. We can do that in the future in terms of administratively addressing some of their issues like bundling and things like that. That wouldn't be in the ordinance anyway. That would be in the EBO, purchasing and CAD side. That can be taken care of without jeopardizing the new opportunities for Small Businesses. So I would say about 90% of their concerns can be addressed. A disparity study can be addressed. While we have the updated ordinance that provides these extra benefits and protects the city against potential liability. I'm not going to give you my full spiel on this. I'm trying to -- we have a busy day. But I think it's very important for you guys to know that what we're doing here today, what the new owner does is all plus. Nothing that has raised concern can't be addressed while we have the new ordinance that provides benefits to the Small Businesses.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Suling and the rest of them, can we make sure we have the timer set for ten minutes. Councilman Carlson.

My question to you, which they raised and put it back out again, can we -- why can't we leave this suspend it and/or is there a way to leave it so that it is easier to bring back if these policies change? The challenge is that if suddenly within a year or two years, these policies change and we need to bring it back, then we have to rebuild everything again. How can we set it up so it's easy to turn it back on?

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: Thank you. Four clarification points. The longer form has this. The way we rewrote this ordinance, we still acknowledge the protected classes. We acknowledge Black Businesses, Hispanic Businesses, lgbt businesses, Veteran Businesses, we acknowledge all those, and we do that because, if after we do studies -- and this is something the department does right now and they'll continue to do. They look and part of what the ordinance Keeps In Place, we're going to continue to do record keeping so we can see where the disparities arise and when we see a sufficient support to move forward with making those changes, all we do is take whichever protected class it is that we see the disparity in and we amend the ordinance to add that class to what's currently under the small business group or eligible business enterprise. It's not a difficult process. It will take no more than a couple of weeks to come to City Council to present the evidence we have that supports the need to address a disparity and to get you to approve the change.

My concern on this, as Councilman Carlson said, it takes things that may be temporary and potentially makes them permanent. I would like to see something that takes the benefit out of this without making permanent some of the things that are potentially a temporary political reality. Nobody, I want to be very clear, nobody is saying we have to be inconsistent with Florida law. Nobody is saying we should act in Any Way that isn't consistent with either applicable Florida law, federal law and so forth but to make things permanent I think gives some pause. I do think we need more time for this. That troubles me because a lot of the good people that we hear today. Mr. Ransom had noted in his remarks a salute to Councilwoman Hurtak for bringing up this issue. I did want to salute for that because you spoke out on this the first time around. I think that's something worth saluting. Always like to do that. It takes something to be a person who speaks out and talks about that. Thank you, ma'am. Again, I do think that we do need more time on this. That's my opinion. We can get the good out of this without making permanent things that maybe aren't permanent. Again, nobody is saying we have to act inconsistent with federal law or state law and so forth, but there may Be Another Way to get there. That's my challenge. Again, thank you.

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: The ordinance is written to address that specific concern. We hope it's not going to be permanent. That's our hope. Nothing in this new ordinance will stop us from doing a disparity study. Nothing in the new ordinance will stop us from doing the current analysis that we do to determine if there are issues that need to be addressed. And nothing in the ordinance will stop us from taking some of the toba recommendations in terms of unbundling, in terms of providing additional support for small businesses, which would include women and minority businesses. The ordinance doesn't do that. The ordinance is really all plus -- just a quick anecdotal story. I just caught a guy out in the hall. He has a Black business. His business is no longer eligible to participate in the program because their revenue is too high. Just a little bit. Not a lot. They are not making hand over fist, but they are a little bit too high to be in our program. This ordinance would allow him to return, be in the program and be able to bid on higher projects. That's what we're looking at.

segments.text: And then from that reporting we find that maybe this is not working, are we able to go back and make changes that are still in accordance with the Florida law?

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: Absolutely. If we find -- first of all, by doing the record keeping we'll be able to, you know, tease out what the problems are and then we can address those directly. segments.text: Just to clarify so we can all be on the same page --

segments.text: Mr. Brody, could you explain the jeopardy the city would be in if we don't pass this?

segments.text: Absolutely. We have several different levels. We have federal level. segments.text: Great. Again, I wanted to start to make sure -- obviously, it is stream important and I wanted to make sure we had people here to answer all questions -- are we having a problem with the Mike or something, Chair?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: No, there's some Hot Mike somewhere reverberating. I don't know where it is.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: I was saying, Nicky Day is on the call. She will help me with questions that you may have. I was definitely focusing on all the documents, certainly, but mostly the issues that related to the city. The document has a lot of requirements for Hillsborough County. Obviously, they will end up owning the ballpark, so I want to make sure, because i'm sure there will be questions that i'm familiar with, but Nicky Day will help me answer some of the questions. I expect the county attorney to be here shortly and the Assistant County Administrator if we have questions. To kind of set the stage, there are three documents that are before you. The most important one that I expect we'll spend our time on is the funding agreement. That's the one that has most of the terms that affect the city. There are two other agreements, non-relocation agreement, that's where they agree that they are not going to relocate and then a guarantee agreement. That guarantee agreement is basically the overall company that owns all the subsidiaries, that the overall company is guaranteeing all the representations and all the commitments that the companies underneath the umbrella company are making. There are three agreements, three resolutions, but I expect that we're going to focus most of our attention today on the development and funding agreement. With that, I'D just like to go back and kind of set the stage a little bit on how we got here. I know there are some concerns or has been concerns about how this has been a pretty quick process. I understand that the City Council passed a motion that wanted to see the agreement Onbase by Friday at 5. It was actually made Onbase about 4:20. Pretty close. I know some people have commented, made the agenda about 4:20 it was published. We did make it in Onbase I think in compliance with the City Council's directive in the motion. After that, we continued to negotiate the document. It was not complete, but really what ended up happening is because there was so much going back and forth, issues that julia and I basically said Tuesday night, again, julia being the county attorney. I went to her office. We sat there with julia, Sam Hamilton, chief assistant, Myself, and Nicky Day, and we basically said we're going to create the document that we can represent to our clients. Tuesday evening we finalized the document, and we presented -- we put it to Onbase and sent it to City Council. That's the document that had all the changes. That's the document that both Myself and the county attorney is going to recommend for their consideration tomorrow for the county commission. Subsequent to that there was one additional change that I submitted that I want to make sure gets approved today, and that is -- it's very important -- when I get to it, i'll explain it, but the payment that we're making that i'll go through the 80 million, 20 million for each fiscal year, is going to be paid based on a reimbursement of completed improvements, public improvements. So it's going to be a reimbursement model. And that language wasn't in the first draft that came out Wednesday morning. So what should be on the record for the City Clerk is the provision that has that reimbursement model. But I passed out -- there were just a couple of tweaks that I would like to make. It reiterates, I highlighted in yellow. It reiterates that provision, payment shall be on a reimbursement basis for completed improvements. That's important to the city because that's always been our issue. Since we're going to address this today, I want to add in the city contribution amount shall be repaid as set forth in exhibit e. It's already in exhibit e that says exhibit e, which we'll discuss later. That's the increment, that the money comes in increment, which i'll come back and explain, will go back to pay for these funds that are going to be paid for the reimbursement. It's simply putting it here so it's there so everyone knows that the money coming back from the increment will be used to pay down that money that is used to reimburse. There is one other change we would like to make. That is, there are conditions for our payment. There's conditions in the agreement before we would make the first $20 million payment, there are a number of conditions. One of those conditions is that the CRA, the county, and the city will enter into the revised second amendment interlocal agreement to effectuate all the CRA issues that are addressed in the agreement. What this does is simply make this one change in the second paragraph that I highlighted simply makes that condition cannot be waived. It cannot be waived. It has to be complied with. With that, just so I get to the end and then i'll come back and talk about the major components that address the city, if you want to move forward today, what I need is a motion -- i'll focus on the development and funding agreement -- a motion to approve the resolution that's before you with these couple of changes and i'm going to address the community benefits agreement shortly. We need to address that issue as well. I would need a motion to approve the resolution, propose these changes and the funding agreement.
