segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: Phoning a friend. Julia Mandell, Hillsborough County attorney. The way the contract -- the agreement is structured is the rays will need to provide us their financial, both their financial information and the guarantees that we've talked about previously prior to any funding that would occur either by the county or the city.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Miranda, does that satisfy your concern?

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: [Inaudible]

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Ms. Mandell, can you restate that?

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: Mr. Miranda has heard me speak on many occasions. He probably just tuned me out. Again, Julia Mandell, Hillsborough County attorney. The way the agreement is structured is the team, the rays will be obligated and their companies, there are a couple of different companies involved in this, will be obligated to provide us their financial information prior to us funding any of our monies either through the county or the city.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: I want to know, how is the Cdd get ITs money and how is it distributed back? To me it's like paying me back with my own money.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: Cdd is going to get the money from the TIF and there's going to be an interlocal agreement between the city, the county and the Cdd that will more narrowly define how that process works. So that agreement will be back in front of City Council.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: That's what I was thinking earlier. The money that goes into the Cdd is actually tax money, isn't it? In a Different Way?

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: Yes, yes.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: They will pay us back with our own money?

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: Pay the city back with money generated by their development --

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: That means they are paying it back with our own money.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: It's how you say it, not I. Councilman.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Don't go anywhere.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: That's money that wouldn't be generated unless we had the development. Councilwoman Hurtak.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Ms. Mandell, you said that we'll get the financials from the rays. What kinds of financials will we be getting?

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: The way it is structured is financials satisfactory to us and our financial advisors.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Which is what?

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: We have very professional financial advisors that actually they are the same for the city and the county. We jointly share the same financial advisors. We will at the time that is appropriate have those folks work with their financial folks to determine what we need to show us and the city, say us, the county, but also the city, that they have the financial capability to proceed forward with this deal and it has to be satisfactory to us.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Will that be made public record?

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: I can't answer that question because it depends on the record. It would depend on whether or not those particular records would have either a confidentiality or exemption under the public records law. It would be defined by that. If they are public records and they come to the Governmental Entities and they become public records. If they have a particular exemption or confidentiality provision in the Florida public records law, then they would not.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Basically we're saying we're going to be using numbers that you all might be able to see but the rest of us cannot.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: I'm not able to answer the question in the way you asked it. I think we would be looking at it in terms of what would be the provisions of the public records law that would apply to whatever document we received.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: As far as public records go, because in the document itself, it mentioned that not all public records will be made available to the public around this deal. Can you explain that a little?

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: I don't know that I would characterize It That Way.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: If it's a public record, it's a public record. We can't contractually change state law. If there's some -- I don't think there's any provision that I recall that says that. But if there is even an indication that that's the case, it's not enforceable. Public records are public records.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: Public records are public records. We are obligated to comply.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: Saying that in stereo.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: It's an important point and I think it's important for the Public to understand, that anything that comes to us as governmental entities will be subject to the Public -- i've made this very clear to the team throughout this process -- those documents which are subject to the Public records law are public records unless there's an exemption or a confidentiality which are two different things under the Public records law. And we will comply with this.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Julia, before you --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: You can try to escape.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Part of the purpose in putting -- setting up the TIF and the cdd is that they are subject to public records and sunshine, correct?

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: Correct.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: The Cdd would be public, same public records requirements --

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Unlike other deals done in the past on essentially tax abatement where it was given just to the developer and we never saw it again, in this case, any money would go to the Cdd, collected in the TIF, then given to the Cdd, subject to public records and sunshine and then the public would have oversight to make sure that the money is only spent in the Right Way and only spent on government-owned infrastructure, not on anything that the rays own, correct?

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: We both agree.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I see one other person. Y'all can go for now. President Barclay, would you mind coming up? I know i'm kind of surprising you. Could you start with your name.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: You represent the police officers in the City Of Tampa.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Have you been satisfied with your conversations with the rays in ensuring public safety on this proposed project?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Have they been working with you in developing what would meet the needs of what your officers require and the City Of Tampa needs? Councilman Viera reached out to us months ago. We've been meeting with Hillsborough County Fire Rescue, TFR here locally and obviously us.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. Appreciate it. Anybody else have any other questions for anybody else? If not, we'll go to public comment. No rays. If they are here to answer questions, if anybody has questions. But no presentation. Are you ready? I'm going to have -- just a reminder that if you wanted to speak to item 80, which is this rays agreement, you should have signed into one of these pages. If you haven't signed into a page, please see a staff member to have your name added to the page. Okay? We're here for a long time today, when you have conversations, the amplification here is just amazing. Our acoustics, whoever designed this was great. We can hear whispers. If you have to have a conversation, if you could take it out into the hall, we'd appreciate it. Mr. Shelby, would you remind folks of the rules of public comment? Because we have new people.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Martin Shelby, City Council attorney. Very briefly, a three-minute time limit applies to all speakers providing public comment. Speakers and members of the public are reminded to please refrain from disruptive behavior, including making vulgar or threatening remarks or making or causing disruptive noises or sounds or displaying signs or graphics. Please direct your comments to the entire City Council rather than individuals. The chair Will rule out of order any person who speaks without being recognized or attempts to address council from outside the speaker area at the lectern. Persons failing to comply with council's rules may also be ruled out of order and at the discretion of the chair may be removed from the chambers and city hall for the remainder of today's meeting. Finally, City Council should refrain from engaging a speaker under public comment. The public should be aware that the City Council does not take questions or have a dialogue during general public comment. This is your opportunity to express your position. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: And a couple of other reminders. This is joint public comment for Tampa City Council and the CRA meeting, special call meeting. If you are to speak to the rays' agreement from either entity, City Council perspective or CRA, this is your opportunity to speak to both the CRA Board and City Council which are the same people. For those of you here to speak for or against or provide any other information, you have three minutes. Don't feel like you have to use the whole three minutes. If you have something to say, of course, we want to hear it. If you are going to say, hey, I support this. Could be sweet, simple, say oppose it, could be short, sweet, simple. If somebody already said what you were going to say, you can say, hey, I agree with what this person said. We're up here listening, right. We would all like to move this along and nobody wants to be here at midnight tonight. I have the names in the order signed in. More sheets coming. I'll call the first few names. As I call you, if you line up against the wall. If you are downstairs or floor two or one and hear your name, please come to Tampa City Council chambers. James Jeffrey, Joe Robinson, Pamela Cannella. Alejandro Noriega. Everybody but james, if you would line up against the wall. Start -- by the way, when you start, if you have never done this before, there is a microphone embedded in the podium, so you have to Face This Way, otherwise nobody can hear you at home and they are watching this. You're addressing City Council and not the audience. Always start with your name. The light will come on. You have three minutes, and then there will be a yellow light when you have 30 seconds left. The yellow light will turn red and that's when I cut you off. Good afternoon, council. Great to be in front of all of you again. To start off, I know public service can be a very thankless job. You have sides on both sides. Either going to vote for you from now on or this vote not going to vote for you. Putting that aside, I want to thank all of you for your hard work, City Staff, County Staff, everybody involved in the process. We know it was a lot of work. I simply come down to have faith in the process we've gone through. That you have faith in the staff, faith in yourselves and in your leadership. We see the potential of this project and the benefits it can bring to the college, too, to the generations that are going to go to that college that now have the opportunity for internships, job training, to the hospitality industry. Just so many benefits of the project. I just want to ask, when you go to bed after your decision, have faith in that decision that in 20, 30, 40 years when you look at your kids, grandkids, children, that when they are graduating from that college and have that internship, they have that job or the workers at the ballpark that you can turn to them and say I was a part of that. I helped their future. I urge you to please say yes to this project. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Joe Robinson followed by Pam Cannella. Joel Robinson. I just want to thank you guys for hearing out the Community. I won't take much of your time. There are a lot of Rays' fans here who will be sharing That Are Way smarter than me. They thought through why this is a great deal for the Community and the taxpayers alike. I'll give them the opportunity to remind you guys of these things. I simply ask you guys this. Have an open mind during this time during the hearing out from the Community. Let go of some of the perceived things you might have had over the past meetings. The leadership of the Rays have done more than enough to move this deal forward. I ask you guys to do the same.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much, Joel. Pam Cannella, Alejandro Noriega, Sandy Sanchez, Patrick Cimino. My name is Pam Cannella. By the way, it's 215 million for a new college. We don't know where the money is coming from. I say no to investing any Taxpayers' money on this project. It's time to give back to the neighborhoods. When the neighborhoods -- sorry. The rays can wait. They can leave or build their own stadium, mixed-use complex. Tampa neighborhoods do come first. Councilwoman Young said her support depended on commitments. I back here. It says community impacts on long-standing needs of district 5, truly affordable and attainable housing, clear definition for student housing, and housing for people to live, work, and play in that community. Quality jobs, opportunities for smart -- i'm sorry -- for small local minority businesses and a concrete commitment written in absolute clarity, transparency, and accountability. I don't see this in the contract. This contract is ambiguous. A legal mumbo jumble. A practice used by companies to cover all their risks in a deal. In this case, all the risks fall on the Taxpayers and no protection for the people. Remember 2024, it seems absurd that for the neighborhoods to receive the funding, that is by right ours for infrastructure, we have to help fund this stadium project. I believe they even want us to ask for maintenance and repairs. This is not about a rays' stadium. It's about Taxpayers funding and other massive mixed use projects for developers and profits, not our profits. Neighborhoods have already helped fund the riverwalk and downtown Tampa. The City Of Tampa neighborhoods have had 16 years of infrastructure and neglect, leaving neighborhoods vulnerable. There are those who are happy because they see in the future of Tampa that. This is what i'm told. But this is what I see for the future of Tampa. More flooding and more flooding and no cleaning. And our water, our drinking water filled with high levels of --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Pamela.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: No, no, no, no Pamela. Broken promises. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: After you finish speaking, if you'll go down to the second floor so we can make room for other public speakers. If you have spoken, please go down to the second floor. Mr. Noriega, good afternoon. Start with your name. You have three minutes. Just to be honest with you, just get it done. At this point, might as well do the deal. You'll have your haters and have your lovers, all flips of the coin, just get the deal done. I remember when this council, certain individuals of the council voted no on raymond james stadium when it was created and that was created and look how that turned out. Certain individuals said no giving millions of dollars to Water Street and look how that development came out to be. This is a good deal no matter how much you think of it. You might not be a sports fan, might not like the rays. In order to grow as a city, build and put money into projects that will help your city. That being said, look at cities like Kansas city, the royals are getting over 70% of their stadium paid by public subsidies by the county and city commissions. And the city didn't have to give them that money. They just said, here you go. Take the money. Because why? They know what it's like losing a major league franchise. I'm all for the deal. I understand everyone has criticism. Again, you'll get both sides of the coin. You'll get yes, no, why, who are we, why are we doing this. At the end of the day when we're all looking back in 30 years, we'll be doing the same thing we do when we go to the lightning stadium, raymond james stadium. We're just going to enjoy the games and be thinking, wow, we actually did this. We made another generational project that will benefit our city for future generations to come. I leave it to you guys. I hope you guys make the right decision. I appreciate you all for letting me speak on this historical day. Thank you very much. Get this deal done for the rays. Please and thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. Sandy Sanchez, patrick, MaryBeth, and Michelle Mastrototaro. My name is Sandy Dediego Sanchez. On August 10 of this year you began a budget meeting with two of you complaining about the mayor and her disrespect for you and your position regarding the $2 billion budget. You had to beg for a hard copy of the budget. You received it after the first presentation at 5:00 on a Friday night. And it was illegible because the print was too small. You said she was guilty of malicious compliance and suggestion and investigation by the Attorney General's Office of the State of Florida might be in order. The definition of malicious compliance is the deliberate literal execution of a directive or policy in a way that satisfies the rule but knowingly undermines ITs intent instead of solving the problem. The two of you that were most vocal on this -- are the same two that have disrespected the taxpayers in the Same Way. You publicized a 134-page document on Friday at 5:00 p.m., Giving the taxpayers of Tampa five days to read and assimilate the information. And now 24 hours before to make a vote you come up with changes which we have not had the opportunity to see but to hear. The only difference between your insult and the mayor's for the $2 billion, there are two to four budget workshops, if you have time to read, digest the information and ask questions and discuss about the budget. Since supposedly can't talk among yourselves, the council that cared about constituents would have entertained the idea of a workshop. Could have had our many questions answered, and you all had certainly received many and many concerns and would like our questions answered. What is unconscionable and irresponsible about these meetings today, you could have waited 37 days for November 4 for the property tax amendment three to see what effect it would have on the decision. The rays have set deadlines and you have passed them over and they are still here negotiating. There is no rush except in the minds of the greedy. How irresponsible of you. How disrespectful of you to the taxpayers of the county. Malicious compliance, you are guilty. Hopefully the Attorney General's Office will investigate. Shame on you. On the same point, the amendment 3 should be predominant in your minds. Please postpone the vote until after November 3rd so can give you more time to review the changes and make rational decisions. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Patrick. My name is Patrick Cimino. Taxpayer and citizen of Tampa. A rays' stadium would be really nice but we have to scrutinize this because it is an extensive expenditure of public access. City, county, and state. And as a taxpayer, we're funding Hillsborough College's new college. This 138-page agreement was released three business days prior to the meeting. Some county commissioners are complaining about they are getting it with even less time. I ask rhetorically, have you read it? Do you understand it? As the stormwater debate has shown, the city is evasive, opaque, and frequently lacks expertise, putting the citizens and taxpayers at risk. Are you comfortable that we've had adequate, independent professional opinions and due diligence? There are gaps too numerous to count. I will focus on the global concerns and add a few specific examples. There is a plethora of public assets mentioned, CIT, CRA, tourist taxes, City and County, bonds, et cetera, now cdd. And stormwater. We pay -- we have to pay for those. It's not just casual that those taxes are coming in. Where is the feasibility studies to support the public debt? Where is the pro forma? I know we got a glimpse of it today for the first time. Cost benefit, risks, opportunity, predictability. The agreement provided last week said the City and County have to consider shifting the CRA. What happens if that doesn't occur in the way that it's required for this agreement? I was involved in proposals, much smaller than this, and had to provide more intensive detail, otherwise the leadership would have told me to get out of here. Who evaluated the credibility of the rays? It says the county in the agreement. What is the credential of them? What did the report say? That's critical. You all are lending them a bunch of money. Why is there so much haste? Is it what's being hidden? What happens if assumptions aren't met? Once demolition and displacement occur, you cannot put toothpaste back in the tube. It's financially irresponsible to proceed with this agreement that is rife with generalities and blanks. Councilor Hurtak did an excellent academic level post debunking with facts and data the myths about benefits of public financing of stadiums like this. And that data has been replicated over decades. Unlike the smoke and mirrors, anyway, I recommend you do not approve this agreement. It's not in the interest of us, the taxpayers.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. Marybeth, michelle, i'm MaryBeth Anglin, president and CEO of the West Tampa Chamber of Commerce. The West Tampa Chamber of Commerce strongly supports the Tampa Bay rays stadium deal and the related development in Drew Park and West Tampa. We believe this is a once in a generation opportunity to keep the rays here in Tampa Bay while creating meaningful long-term investment in our community. This project can create thousands of jobs, attract significant private investment, generate economic activity and create new opportunities for residents and businesses throughout our region. Drew Park and West Tampa are uniquely positioned to benefit from this investment of this magnitude. It can serve as a catalyst for continued revitalization, strengthen local businesses and create opportunities for generations to come. We also strongly support Hillsborough College being the central part of this investment. Education, workforce development must advance alongside economic development, so local residents are prepared to take advantage of these new opportunities that this deal will bring. On behalf of the West Tampa Chamber of Commerce, we encourage the Tampa City Council to move forward with confidence and seize this historic opportunity. We are proud to support keeping the Tampa Bay rays in our region and creating lasting benefits for Drew Park, West Tampa and greater Tampa Bay community. Thank you for your time.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, MaryBeth. Thank you for being short and concise. Michelle Mastrototaro followed by amy. My name is Michelle Mastrototaro. I'm here to -- wow, this has divided so many of us. It's breaking my heart. So heartbroken because you got one side that it's a good thing. You've got the other side, people need addressing. This is a rush. We don't know why it's rushed. The whole proposal had to be revamped back into -- it hasn't even been shown to the public yet. I believe everyone who says, he couldn't even give us any info on anything. He didn't know nothing. He couldn't even tell us what was money -- well -- but i'm saying is that it's a frill. If you remember louis -- can't talk -- USF got their stadium done, Sga, Student Government -- my daughter was a part of it. She had to give them $3 million to build the stadium. I'm thinking why can't we all just figure something out in the best interest because it's half and half. The taxpayers are suffering, and everyone knows. A lot of people lost everything. To put a stadium, it's going to be a big cluster -- cluster of traffic. We want it. I'm not opposed to it. I am for it. But the taxpayers are going to be the ones that suffer. I'm not going to see it. It's going to be 30 years. Think about everybody. I'm all for you all, what you agree or disagree on, but I think we need to come back to the table with the final version of this so we can all be on the same table and we can all agree and make everybody happy and it's fair. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, michelle. Amy Scott, Michelle Dyson. I'm Amy Scott. I came up here and I actually had all my notes on my phone and I actually -- i've been here for a while and i've listened to everything. I do not envy your position because you have the people who are for the rays. They are positioning it where it's very hard to argue with their position. The people who are against it, it is very hard to argue against their position. What we are asking you to do is vote for the reality. The reality is, you guys don't have enough information. I sat in this room and I heard one of these attorneys say that they were just working on documentations on Tuesday. They couldn't answer questions. Hillsborough County Community College, God bless him, he doesn't even have a written commitment that he's going to get the funds that he said he's going to get. We don't have an understanding of how all the money is moving. We are putting ourselves in a position as a city to start being a lender, what door does that open? How do you tell other businesses who say, hey, we now want a cdd, you don't know what that looks like because most of you guys found out what a cdd is on Tuesday, Wednesday or today. I just don't think that you guys are in enough of a position to honestly vote, and then we're not even going to talk about the elephant in the room. A couple of them. One, amendment 3. We don't know what that looks like. If we ever, heaven forbid, another Helene or milton, does the city really have enough money to therefore help the residents of the city out or is it now going to be tied up in a development that they are not willing -- they are not going to be able to take care of because that's not their role? Do we have enough money to loan? I've always been under the mindset you don't loan money that you don't have. So because you might not get it back. There are just a lot of holes when you guys were asking the questions. It looks like we're not going to get back all of our money and spending more than we have. Again, you don't know if that is fact because you just found this information out. If you go to a multimillion dollar home that you want to buy, you have to show financials before you even get shown the house. Yet we don't have financials from the rays. We don't have a full plan of knowing exactly what it's going to do. I am just asking, take a beat. Wait until the 3rd because this is your legacy. None of you will be sitting on council by the time all of the revelation of what this turns out to be comes to pass. You do not want people remembering you as the people who screwed the city 20 years ago. So you need to take a moment and actually make sure you fully understand so that your grandkids or your kids who are running around don't walk around in shame because you are the ones who made their situation worse. Just take a beat. I was coming up here with a very strict plan. But I honestly don't know how you make a decision when you don't have full information. So thank you for your time and, again, I know it's not an easy decision but take a beat.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Michelle Dyson. Stephen Gerhard, Jim Davidson, Carmen Edmonds. Michelle Dyson. I am currently a bartender at Tropicana Field. I've never really been in politics or public spoke until this. It's definitely taught me a lot. There seems to be a little bit of a double standard. I have empathy for all the community, the working class people. I am a working class person, and I definitely support helping people. But empathy can't override common sense. Every meeting I stand here -- I mean, I stand here listening to people at this podium talk keywords like affordable housing, nonprofit, anything free, and it seems like we hand those monies off with a lot of ease. I don't see any financials. I don't see a lot of vetting. Things have to be done. But then when a private partner comes and steps up to the plate offering over a billion dollars to bring massive income growth, thousands of jobs, it switches gears. We hold their feet to the fire. We're stalling. We scrutinize. We ask this, this, this, continual. It's really easy for you to give money to -- entity but so difficult for you to accept a massive private investment. We can't hate the wealthy. They give money. They invest in us. They give us jobs. Instead, I would like to thank all of you for listening to the community, especially Ken Babby who I had the opportunity to work with, for negotiating, staying at the table, keeping the deal alive. We've been waiting, people like, oh, it's only been this long or that long. But it's been 20 years. Between St. Pete and over here, people have been trying to work this out. I think now is the time to do it for us, for the working class, for the taxpayers. In my job as a bartender, if somebody comes up and says, hey, can you pour me a drink but they don't give me any money, I have to say, let me see the card. I think the over billion dollars that they showed us is a good reference for the facility that we should have. I hope we stop pushing away the big investment and approve the Rays' deal to protect our livelihoods, bring our jobs and housing to the working class. We can't mislead these people that if we don't spend the money on this they are going to get the money because that is not the truth. You know that and I know that. It's important that we still listen to everybody that we do what is best for the future and hopefully I have a job for always until my time leaves this earth that I can work at the Rays. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. John. John byzek. John, if you are downstairs and hear this, please come to the council chambers and make yourself known. I will call you when you get up here. Stephen. I spent a lot of time on the phone with several of you. Don't envy the position you are in. Stephen Gerhard, homeowner and resident of Hillsborough County. I hope to hold a masters in sports management and mba. Started my career with the Tampa Bay Lightning and spent nearly a decade in professional sports. Seven years ago I transitioned to commercial real estate. I am uniquely prepared to comment on what is presented at the matter at hand. A phrase you have heard thrown around. Economic impact. Economic impact is the total dollars generated by a development. You have been handed a gross number in the aecom report. Counts every dollar that moves. Net impact asks the harder question. How many of those dollars are new? This is not a fringe topic in sports literature, it is one of the most consistently studied questions in sports economics and decades of peer research across every major league finds almost no measurable gain from publicly financed stadiums. The reason is simple, substitution. Family spend $300 at the stadium is no longer going to spend $300 on Hyde Park, ybor, up at busch gardens. The money moved. It didn't multiply. The aecom study never test for substitutions. Report lacks several important considerations. Frankly, why are we surprised. Commissioned by the Tampa Sports Authority, the entity that would manage the asset. Last week, Aecom Hunt Turner was selected as the construction manager for the project. Let me connect the DOTs here. The same company whose analysis is being used to justify the subsidy now stands to earn millions of dollars from the construction management fee, $2.3 Billion stadium. It's not an independent study. It's a sales document. I could stop there, but the definitive documents ask the city to advance $20 million on a four-year -- that's $80 million paid by tax increments inside of a district where the team carries no binding or dated obligation to deliver a single square foot of taxable office, hotel, or retail. No reasonable lender on earth funds against collateral that does not exist with no completion guarantee and no delivery covenants. The high to low projections do not matter if we do not deliver taxable land improvements. On $80 million loan, aaa muni bonds somewhere between 5%. Four and a half million dollars debt service obligation there. To deliver that, we'd have to create $355 million of actual retail value. Inside of what was agreed there is 100 to 250 thousand square feet of office. At the end of the day, I want to challenge you to do this. Don't vote for empty promises. Cdd will be controlled by the landowner. Landowner is hcc. Who elects to the board that --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Why are we here today? We're here because neither the mayor, this council, or the BOCC could not walk away from making this deal. You could have told the rays it's fine. Great deal. But the people have to vote first. In fact, the very construction of the previous deal and this deal and the board of county commissioners deal, the CRAs, the cdds, the special districts, the horizontal improvements, it was all an economic gymnastic event structured so that taxes, in this case property taxes, could be given away without requiring a referendum. You as a Tampa City Council could not do that. You had to disguise it under the cdd and a special taxing unit and TIF it. By the way, Kansas city who passed it, used a TIF. The people voted it down in Kansas city the year before they had to do that. Amendment 3 is on the election ballot in ten weeks. Raise your hand if you think Tampa can afford this contract to pass, if it passes. Any of you up there, raise your hand if you think that this city can afford to do this, if the amendment pass.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: We don't do that. There are requirements to fund different revenue streams if one stream does not meet the required contributions. The Rays are loaning the city money so you can build their stadium and pay it off with our property taxes. Are you kidding me? Transformation has said a lot. It is not. This is window dressing. Amendment 3 is transformational, increasing the number of county commissioners, compositions of the BOCC, and real term limits would be transformational. This is transformational, increasing people's properties who were taken because they couldn't pay their property taxes. And this thing you are discussing today is not going to make that any better. It's going to make it worse. Don't even begin to talk about financial impacts because as the gentleman said, insulting to tell people that crap when you know it's not true. And then give them a chance, and not give them a chance to vote on it. Used car salesmen have better standards. And I apologize to any used car salesmen in the room. You also know the deal is not the end of the Rays taking money from us. It's in the document. Why did the Rays give all the money to politicians running for office? Who can't vote on the deal, because they are going to continue to ask for money for years. You all know it. It's in the document. This is a bad economic deal. A bad political deal and morally bad deal. You are all adults. You know the consequences. It's time to do the right thing. Vote no.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Carmen Edmonds, Laura Lawson, Ron Weaver, Doug Battista. Carmen, start with your name. Just to go on the record, I want everyone to know, there are about 20 to 30 college students upstairs with the lovely Tampa Bay backpacks that are leather. Several of them got them and they were given a little reception at lunch. For people to think there are all these college kids here, I don't believe it for a second. I think they are being used. That's my personal opinion. I digress. I copied a meme from Bernie Sanders a few weeks ago. 31 out of 32 owners of billionaires. 26 out of 30 Mlb owners are billionaires. Your tax dollars help build their stadium. Today, the average person can't afford the price of a ticket to a sporting event. That must change. I'm a very staunch republican. Never in my life would I have ever thought I would be agreeing with Bernie Sanders. We as Taxpayers do not want our money going to fund a Billionaire's pet project. Opposition to the stadium is all about CIT, CIT, it doesn't matter what bucket of money it comes from, it's taxpayer money, whether you take it from this bucket, that bucket or another. We do not want our tax dollars going to fund a Billionaire's stadium. That's not good use of our tax dollars. We have people that have had historical flooding. Our sewers are backed up. Our roads are in disrepair. The money needs to go where it belongs. Another Florida politics article dropped trying to debunk Councilwoman Hurtak's wonderful video she released. Thank you for the video. Very informational. One item continues to be true. Mixed use stadium developments elsewhere failed to pay back Taxpayers. This article said that the deal, that the Tampa deal is going to be different. But to me, that's like Democrats in Washington telling all of americans that socialism is going to be different this time because it's in america. It's never worked anywhere. This deal is not going to work here. Socialism is not going to work in america. It never works anywhere. That's just ridiculous. Don't sell us a bag of goods. Another Councilman stated on social media that local officials have done exactly what Taxpayers elected them to do. Have you? I don't know of any taxpayer that elected you to give away a billion dollars collectively of our money to a Billionaire for a stadium. You all are caving to the rays and higher up elected officials. Do what's right for voters and vote no. Put it on the ballot and let Taxpayers decide the fate of our money. We don't want to fund a stadium. We don't want to fund a new FDLE and tax assessor's office. The buildings are practically brand-new, run very efficiently. I don't know why we are tearing them down when they are perfectly fine. That's double dipping taxpayer money. Built ten years ago or less. Now tearing it down and building again with more taxpayer money. That is a misuse of our money. It's ridiculous. I think this needs to go back on the ballot for Taxpayers to decide. I ask you to please vote no today on all of this stuff.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Laura Lawson followed by Ron Weaver. It is uniform. I'm Laura Lawson. I'm resident of Tampa, south Seminole Heights. I have been afraid that Ken Hagan was going to pull this off for about a decade. Like, I felt it in my body, like worried about it. The ybor deal. I was scared of that. We can't afford this. I've also -- the whole time I worked for commissioner Pat Kemp, always dealing with him down the hall. We knew he was scheming to try to pull this off and give away all our tax dollars for a team we couldn't afford. I worried about it. I read all kinds of books about it. They showed a clear pattern about how these things work. This is how they work. You avoid a public vote. Rush approval of the financial deal through local boards and councils. You provide rosy projections about economic impact that never pan out. And you make it a quest to get a team rather than a careful consideration of the relative cost to taxpayers, and in this case, to our public assets versus benefits to the community. I never expected they would take a college. I've literally been anxious about this for a decade. I never expected that to happen. I came here on May 22 and I made a very clear -- I want to add the djj to this, by the way, because I didn't know about that yet. I'm so tired of chasing down information. I spent the weekend looking at all those documents. Anyway, I came in and I gave you a list of things I wanted to see in the public benefits agreement. I wanted to you build the college back first. If we have to tear it down for this plan, why is it that the rays get to move from one stadium to a fresh, brand-new stadium. The students have to hang out in trailers for a while and see if they can find Pico Funds at the legislature which have been going down for years because we don't have phone lines anymore. I'm also really worried about this aspect of it. The College Board, which I visited yesterday, those are all appointed by Governor Desantis. They are going to be completely in charge of this property. By agreeing to this deal, we're handing over to the college a mixed use project, and they are going to be in charge of whatever goes in there. Notice, you cannot require anything. This council cannot require anything. The other thing that I learned at that meeting was that the college is going to be asking for 164 -- $165 million from the legislature this coming year in these Pico Funds, which have to go to Charter Schools, regular schools. They may not have enough money to replace the college, even under the plan that they put forward. So vote no. Bring it into this. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Laura. Ron Weaver, Doug Batista -- respectfully, I think you need to vote yes. Despite all that we've heard, the alleged 300 family diversion to Hyde Park has five huge holes in the argument and studies in columbus, Ohio, and sacramento, California, that as long as you have a mixed use project, it is the opposite with respect to their alleged studies where they have taken exceptions with no mixed use and recessionary economies that didn't work. Sacramento, California, columbus, Ohio, and other mixed use projects like L.a. Live and dozen others show that the economic -- even if only half of the 56 billion comes to bare, 7% sales tax on it is 2 or $3 billion per 30 years, $8 billion of sales taxes just in the next century alone. 12,000 new jobs we won't otherwise get. That 300 Hyde Park diversion -- a lot of folks are from out of town to view the game. They are not going to --

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: You have to Turn This Way. Thank you. Vote yes because, number one, america's pastime may be baseball. Community and oneness and unity is america's lifeline. Number two, it will encourage corporate relocations. Number three, 12,000 jobs we otherwise will not get. Number four, it will speed rail up, maybe by as much as a decade with 10 million visitors a year. That's going to be something like a billion visitors per century. Those visitors Will Help Drive rail here earlier, maybe as early as a decade earlier. Number five. The nature of the pride that we take in our community, the ability to get it done. If Monsignor Higgins and george and leonard levy and Mcewen looking down at the obstacles they overcame to do the impossible, to show the pride of this community, they would want us to take the can-do-ness that is Tampa and remember that when Tampa has the opportunity to help ITs citizens with 12,000 jobs they would not otherwise get and 10 million visitors per year to the economy that they would step up to the plate because this community believes in ITs people. It believes in getting jobs for ITs people. It believes in Hillsborough College. Hillsborough College needs for us to take the State of Florida -- the way we solve this issue, we can solve rail. If we solve rail, we can solve health care. If we solve health care, we can solve insurance rates. We can solve it with a Solvent Wealth Fund with respect to -- tourist development dollars. We can do the things the community has to do if we start right here with a transformational, once in a lifetime opportunity to get us the 12,000 jobs we would not otherwise get, to show our children that when things matter, we can get it done and that those 10 -- can be our economy, our Volunteers --

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Thank you very much. My name is Doug Batista. For my career, I am a chief human resources officer. I have extensive experience in labor force dynamics with some of the world's largest companies. In the united states we're losing 16,000 net jobs per month. About $200,000 annually due to a.i. Displacement. That includes accounting for the a.i. Jobs being created. Those are net. That was done by a study by Goldman Sachs. The jobs that are being displaced are those with routine, repetitive, administrative tasks such as accountants, computer programmers, testers, customer service, and entry level roles. I'm living this in my current company right now as chief HR officer. These are not huge job losses right now. Few hundred thousand jobs across the united states. Not a huge amount of jobs about but a.i. Impact on the job market is expected to continue. All you need to do is read some of the studies out there by global firms like McKenzie. If you don't believe that, there is another warning sign. Mercer Consulting and U.s. Bureau of Labor Statistics report that voluntary employee turnover has collapsed to 13%, down from 25% three years ago. This isn't because workers are suddenly more satisfied with their jobs. Rather, employees are standing as a direct consequence of fewer job opportunities. Again, I am seeing the same exact trends with my current employer. If you don't believe that, maybe you'll believe bill gates. Yesterday, he published an article and it was picked up on the Wall Street Journal and New York Times. He quoted, we have to think now about how to reduce job losses so that everyone can share in the prosperity that a.i. Creates. Waiting until people are already displaced or underemployed will be too late, end quote. The rays' stadium and mixed use development projects represents job opportunities for the Tampa Bay work force in a time of a.i. Displacement. Jobs provide financial stability for working families across our region, including the thousands of jobs that will be created. More important than being an HR executive, i'm a dad. I'm a dad -- my son has developmental and mental health challenges. He struggles, he has an intense fear of being around others. He was once a mute and wanted to be invisible. His medical team prescribed emergent therapy to overcome the fear and recommended that we take him to a rays' game. He came fixated with what was happening on the field instead of the major anxiety around all the people. Baseball became his vehicle to recovery. Today his love of the team and the game of baseball drives his daily life. Here is a photo of him drawing in art class, art class that he was failing until I got him an iep at his school. He now draws stadiums like this and provides me with dug-outs of tropicana field. In closing, I ask the City Council to vote yes for job creation and for my son and any other special needs kids out there. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, doug. Melanie Alvarez. Julie Magill. James Ransom, Jeffrey Johnson, Michael Maurino. Or afternoon. We've been here a long day. Thank you all for sticking it out with us. I'm Melanie Alvarez. I am a grateful floridian, and i'm speaking on behalf of Americans for Prosperity Tampa Bay today. I want to start by saying we're not here because we're against the rays or a stadium, but we are here because we believe that the people's voice in a multimillion dollar deal is very important and public/private partnerships matter. So right now, you have a decision that will affect this community for 35 years potentially, and that decision is being made without the impact of people, with the exception of public comment. Those are the people that are going to be paying for it and bearing the risk of it. So let's be clear about what's happening. You all know the numbers but both sides are making a bet on future growth. And the public's bet is locked in for 35 years through a Tax Increment Financing District that freezes revenues to schools, fire services, and city budgets. And we're unclear about the implications of amendment 3 as other people have said. Not a small decision. A generational decision. It deserves really close public scrutiny and it also deserves transparency and documents that have been released this week really don't allow time for that to happen as other people have said. We need more time. Economic research has consistently shown negative or neutral growth or economic impact with stadiums. And the independent analysis of tax increment financing finds they rarely deliver the net growth that they promise. These are not opinions. These are from peer reviewed research. So maybe this stadium will be different. Maybe the growth projections will come true. But if it's not the case, shouldn't voters be confident enough to take the question to the ballot. If you as council people believe in the deal and the community you are serving, we should trust people to vote on it. Instead we're asking residents to accept a 35 year commitment with possible added taxes in the future based on projections they may not approve or trust. We still don't have clarity on our city's budget in the future with implications of amendment 3. That's not how we should do business with public dollars. Documents and changes to the deal continue to flow in until Tuesday night providing this council and the county commission very little time to review the finite points. We don't even know that these are the finalized documents which really calls transparency into question. I urge you to do the right thing. Do not make a 35-year bet with taxpayer dollars. Let the residents decide or postpone this until after the amendment 3 ballot and we know the outcome of that in November. Thank you for your time.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Melanie. Julie Magill followed by James Ransom. Start with your name. You have three minutes. My problem with this deal is the contract. Numerous times throughout this contract it uses the word contribution. Contribution, and this is going to end up, let's say this does go to litigation, falls apart. Any lawyer is going to look at that word and say, you know what? That is a contribution. That is not an expected repayment. So here is your definition of contribution. The other things I have a problem with are the fact that they are asking us to do all the maintenance and repairs on that stadium. That could come to $15 million a year. I don't understand why that is even in the contract. That needs to be just done away with. There's also blanks in the contract still. I don't see how you can vote on something that is not a complete contract yet. There's just too many issues. Too many ambiguities in this contract. There should be a hard cap on Tampa's total exposure. A maximum dollar amount, not 80 million plus, plus, plus, plus because we don't know. It's ridiculous. If Tampa is protected in that contract, show me where, because I don't see it. The county shortfall shouldn't be a Tampa problem. If the county doesn't come through with the money, are we guaranteed they are not going to look to us for it? Too many questions. I agreed with everything everybody else said. I won't take the whole three minutes because I know everybody wants to go home. Take a look at the checklist. I e-mailed it to you. Now you have another hard copy.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: James, followed by Jeffrey Johnson and Michael Maurino. My name is James Ransom. I'm again representing the economic development committee for the Tampa Organization of Black Affairs. There have been a lot of things said today and over the course of this process. Our hope is that the City Council and the mayor, the county commission, the county administrator has taken a good look at all the details that concern the public, public trust, public money, and do the right thing about that. Otherwise, toba supports the rays coming to Tampa. I can tell you haven't met anyone over 46 years that spent more time in the Black community and around the City Of Tampa than Ken Babby coming out and talking to people in the community about this issue. Doesn't mean everything he's saying, buy into and this kind of thing. You have to figure all that out. But the work was done to come face to face so they could hear what people's concerns are. We're here laser focused on the special interest of the Black community without any ambiguity and you know that. But it is toward the betterment of the entire community. We don't want to be excluded from whatever prosperity might be generated from this great transformative project. We want to also enjoy the heightened quality of life that can come from the project. We think the president of Hillsborough College did a good job explaining how that benefits students in the college. Construction and changes take time and very inconvenient. Once all that might be done, if done right, it may be one of the best things we could ever do in our community. It has to be done with a fiscally responsible leadership from your group and the county commission. We would say from the top down, bottom up, share this with Major League Baseball, Mr. Babby and his team, Hillsborough College, the board of county commissioners, and you and the mayor, that top-down, bottom up. We want to see the diversity that represents our people, our segment of the communities in whatever you decide to do if it goes through. Remember we are taxpayers and vote and we happen to be African American people and the city is very diverse. We want to benefit from whatever happens, if it's going to happen with a project of this scale and scope. But to end, we do think it would be wise to find the right path for the right reasons, for the right public trust and protect the public money to have the rays in Tampa, Florida, where they should have been from the beginning in the First Place. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Jeffries Johnson, Michael Maurino, Rick Fernandez. I would like to address you as the CRA Board and not just City Council. Jeffrey Johnson. I serve as the chair of the East Tampa CRA. I'm not representing our committee, but i'm speaking as an advocate of East Tampa. I am here today in support of the extension of the East Tampa CRA. I am not an economist, so I am not a subject matter expert to speak on the entirety of the development and funding agreement that piques the interest of the majority of the persons that are in this room. I am grateful that council sees the need to include an extension of the interlocal agreement between the county and the city and the East Tampa CRA. The East Tampa CRA, East Tampa has made significant progress but our development work is far from finished. We continue to face challenges related to affordable housing, infrastructure, economic development, and commercial revitalization and creating opportunities for long-term residents, homeowners, and businesses. East Tampa CRA was established in 2004. If we are extending ITs life through 2044, then I believe we should also be committed to the funding development through 2044. That's why I want to make an important distinction. I support the extending of the life of the CRA, but we must also protect the funding that gives that extension meaning. I respectfully ask that the City Of Tampa not to remove ITs TIF contribution after 2034, but to instead to continue ITs investment throughout the extension period. On page 28 and 29, it indicates that the county won't fund ITs portion beyond the scheduled 2034 time period. Right now, the county contributes 80% and retains 20% of the TIF for this CRA. The City Of Tampa contributes 100 percent of ITs increment. I encourage the city to negotiate with Hillsborough County so that the county continues or resumes ITs TIF participation through 2044. If we're talking about a 40-year redevelopment horizon, then we should be Planning for fully funded 40-year redevelopment strategy. An additional ten years should not simply keep the East Tampa CRA alive on paper. Those ten years should give us the resources and the opportunity to make transformational investments in the people, the neighborhood, the businesses, and the future of East Tampa. State statute not only allows a max of 40 years of that CRA -- so today I support the extension but I ask this council to go further to protect the city's TIF commitment, negotiate for continued county participation, and ensure East Tampa has the financial resources necessary to finish the work that we've started.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, sir. Michael Maurino, Rick Fernandez, Terrence and todd -- Michael Maurino, executive director Westshore Alliance. We have spoken to you and provide you with our justification for why we support the economic -- potential economic impact, potential impact on infrastructure. I wanted to talk about specifically that dale mabry corridor. You think of Hillsborough down to columbus. It's not as -- don't have the type of economic generation there because a lot of publicly owned land. Also low density. A project with what the rays propose, that starts to change that. You've seen other parts of the city where investments have been made and the scale of this is why having a public investment makes sense. Potential return on investment, whatever it may be makes sense because of the scale and size of the project. You've already done the work in terms of land use Planning, transit Planning for that corridor, but you need to have the investment in it. Large enough investment that will help create the change and we think why it would be viable for City Council and obviously BOCC to support this as well. The thing is moving forward if you are to support today, there's got to be a lot of work that makes this a success so we want to work with you. Planning Commission, City Council, obviously you all, and BOCC but also other entities involved that can help make a success. 35 year project. All that work can be done provided that you have your support today. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Rick Fernandez. Terrance, todd, ct. Today. Rick Fernandez, Tampa Heights Civic Association president. I'm here in a representative capacity today. We are very aware of the significance of this project and this deal. Believe me, we're not living in some rabbit hole. However, we are concerned about a proposed diversion of 50% of Downtown CRA funds. Comments, unlike some heard to this point are going to be more surgical and more specific to a neighborhood. This will hurt the redevelopment of the north portion of downtown, which is a current gap in the urban fabric connecting Tampa Heights. Further, the reduction of the Downtown CRA funds may prevent the expansion of the streetcar, negatively impacting Tampa Heights. The streetcar expansion is identified in the ria, or the regional infrastructure accelerator, and CRA funding will be essential to ITs success. We are asking this council and the CRA Board -- sorry, this council sitting as CRA Board to take one of the following actions in this order of preference. First, do not permit the diversion of Downtown CRA funds for this deal. Second, if diversion is being considered, do not allow it until the streetcar extension is operational and our community has the transit connection that has been promised. Third, if Downtown CRA funds will be diverted, secure $200 million of the streetcar extension, or for the streetcar extension before a single dollar is redirected. In any scenario, expand the Tampa Heights CRA east to the East Tampa CRA boundary and north to the Floribraska Avenue. Our neighborhood has requested this boundary to be extended for nearly a decade. Our neighborhood deserves protections meant to address affordable housing, transit infrastructure, and the kind of long-term investment our community has awaited for decades. I thank you very much. Respectfully submitted. There was an e-mail submitted to all of you I believe Wednesday evening. I incorporate that by reference as part of the record. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, rick. Terrance. Sorry if I slaughtered your last name. My name is Terrance O'sullivan. I'm a member -- a resident of South Tampa. Thank you for the opportunity to address the council on this very important issue. Bottom line up front, we probably should have had a separate meeting just dealing with this as opposed to number 80 on the agenda. It is very important. Everybody's great comments and analysis bears witness to that. Maybe if we continue, depending what you do at your voting, have a separate issue just to discuss this. Really get people understanding. Couple of things, probably redundant what you heard before. First of all, for all my baseball friends, I love baseball. I grew up with it. I played it, and even saw Mickey Mantle hit his 500th home run one time, so i'm dating myself. But I love the rays. But we're talking about business here. So let's get into it. But we must first aggressively analyze the financial details. We talked to some of that and some of the gaps that you pointed out councilwoman. Hey, what does that really mean? You must highlight the details of the pluses and down-sides to this huge and impactful project. 30 plus years, it will be our legacy. I.e., The tax increase financing over 35 years. Getting ahead of myself. Start throwing out terms, CIT, CRA, define what it means, probably get a lot of different definitions. Some of that needs to be highlighted. What is the so what to the Taxpayer? What is the risk to the Taxpayers? We need to clearly know for transparency. That's been pointed out several times. We all want the same thing. Want the community to be developed. Good thing for our lives, our kids' lives but we want to do it the Right Way. This is an opportunity without rushing in to do this. Please -- carefully on this. We know it is a difficult decision. But don't rush to judgment. Please don't do that. Bottom line, this is not a good deal for the current and future Taxpayers from what I know. If we do more critical examination on this. Please help me to help you. Transparency, we're rushing again into this monumental project. Please take a look at that through town hall meetings and whatever marketing we can do on this. Public service announcement may be in order. I feel at this point that we have a shell game that's going on with CIT, CRA, TIF, whatever other acronym come up with today. Please, let's get that done. I feel right now that the developer is winning and the Taxpayer is losing. Thank you for your support. Good luck.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Start with your name, please. Let's get down to business. I put a hundred million dollars in the City Of Tampa since 1986. My first job was selling cokes at the old sombrero at 14 years old. You're going to tell me that the old sombrero when we had the Buccaneers go 0 and 26 and Doug Williams came and one game away from going to the super bowl was a waste of money? You're going to tell me when we built raymond james stadium and got all the jobs for african americans, I grew up with blacks in the bronx before I came here in 1973. In 1973, there was no rays, no bucs, no lightning. When Phil Esposito said we would have hockey at amalie arena, stamkos and those guys got it done and won a stanley cup. You're going to tell me that was a waste of money, too? Get out of my face. People talking here, you don't even know what you're talking about. You don't even know what you're talking about. Hcc needs a remodel. Hcc dale mabry, 162 ball games over there. 81 home ball games plus venues over there. Even talk about the tax money. Make so much money, it's ridiculous. It's ridiculous. I took a guy who never ran for dogcatcher, that would be Donald Trump and put him in the White house. Don't tell me about politics when you don't know anything about. Bernie Sanders hasn't had a job in forever and he's a communist making millions of dollars with three houses on the taxpayer dime. You want to talk business. Let's talk business. This is a deal you got to get done. It's a must get done. It's for the jobs. It's for the community. It's for putting Tampa on the map. We are toe to toe with the New York Yankees, the greatest franchise in sports history and we're three games up with 30 some odd games left. I want to see you boys get it done. We didn't work all this time for you to collapse down the stretch. We didn't work all this hard to get you City Council or the county commission to close and collapse down the stretch either. We're champions. We're the city of champions and that's what we'll always be. I'm Todd Seeme.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. [ sounding gavel ] start with your name. You'll have three minutes. My Name Is Ct Harris. I'll be a little calmer. Just bear with me. First, I want to thank Councilwoman Hurtak for taking the time to break this incredibly complicated deal down into information the public could actually digest through video because regardless of where we stand, transparency does matter. Let me be clear. I want the rays in Tampa. I support economic development. I want Tampa to grow. We can't stop it. Economic growth is powerful. However, growth cannot come at the expense of the people who already call Tampa home. My concern is the speed at which the public has been expected to understand the people's business. We're talking about billions of dollars, future agreements, infrastructure, transportation, community benefits, and obligations that could impact tampanians for generations and long after many of you would transition out of your seats. Yes, this deal has improved, I acknowledge that. But there are still questions. Our roads are already beat down by many cars, many trucks, construction vehicles, and just about anything else with wheels. What happens when thousands of more people are coming in and out of this area, what will the interlocal agreement obligate taxpayers to tomorrow? I mean, we have questions. Most importantly, are the community benefits measurable, enforceable, and meaningful enough to ensure that longtime tampanians can actually benefit, because I don't want Tampa waking up on Christmas morning after being promised all these beautiful gifts only to discover we have a gorgeous tree, aka, the stadium, but nothing underneath it. Or worse we can't even travel to grandma's house because we didn't adequately prepare the infrastructure around it. That Christmas dream can quickly become a taxpayer nightmare. Council, I know the weight on your shoulders today is not light. You've been screamed at, talked about, I get it. Many of you love your roles and you ran for a particular reason. We elected you because we trusted you. We believed you would ask the difficult questions and make the difficult decisions when Tampa needed you most. I'm not asking you to vote against the rays. I'm asking to you protect Tampa while you build Tampa. Make sure our small minority women and veteran owned businesses have real opportunities with these contracts, protect our neighborhoods, demand accountability, address our infrastructure, and make sure promises come with measurable outcomes and consequences. A stadium can absolutely be a part of Tampa's future, but when this deal is finished, don't just make sure Tampa got a stadium. Make sure tampanians got a deal. And I mean a real deal.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Stephanie Poynor followed by Robin Lockett. Stephanie Poynor. This vote should Not Take Place until after November 5. Just that simple. Everybody up there is my friend. I will be the first person to tell you that. All my friends sitting up there. Yeah, whatever. Don't get started with me. Bottom line is you are all my friends and you have to make a really, really difficult decision. No Matter Which Way you vote, there are going to be people in the room that vote against you. Not the thousands of votes i've seen you make. Not the thousands of votes you make every year that you are in office, but this one thing, which just makes me sick. I told most of you this. I am sick and tired of talking about the Rays. We have a $2 billion budget that needs to be discussed and we're spending our time talking about this nonsense because there is a japanese bullet train. Hey, guess what, the mayor must want it because that's what happens every single time. When people are pushing so hard for something like this and have to have it done today, there's nothing okay about it. The fact that we did not get the final copy in Onbase until after 2:30 yesterday, not okay. That right there should be a no vote today. Not yes or no. I'm talking about don't even vote on it because it was not in Onbase last Friday. I don't care who had it. I don't care if the city attorney had it, the county attorney had it, if it was anybody else, you would say we're not voting on this. How many times have you guys had that discussion and said we're not going to vote on it if it's not in there Friday afternoon by 5:00. The first version was, the watered down version that didn't have anything in it about that it was a loan. Anything in there that protected the city. It was all whatever the Rays wanted. I have a whole list of questions. I will e-mail them to you later. Here's what gets me. Councilman Carlson and I both have seniors in high school at home. We will unbridle them from this debt when they are 59 or 60, depending on how old they are. 59 or 60. My daughter who is 17 years old will have this noose around her neck until she is 59. Give me a break. That's ridiculous. For a game which is touted by a bunch of misogynistic jerks on facebook, next door, it's all Over The Place. The way these people are disrespectful and rude to anybody who disagrees with them is absolutely unconscionable. It would be a reason to vote no in and of itself. Just The Way they have talked to people about this. It's a game. They talk to people about it when they say, oh, I don't know like they are beating on their children. This is a game, except to the Billionaires who want all our money. Except for the people who are not getting affordable housing in any of these contracts. Except for the people who are going to make 8 bucks an hour working for the Rays.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Robin Lockett and then a request from council to take a break. After robin, we'll have a 15-minute break. Hard 15-minute break. Please be back in your seats. Robin Lockett, three minutes, kick us off to a break. First, I want to say that I am in support of this, the ending of this deal. I think about the 11,900 jobs. I think about the affordable housing. I think about the infrastructure. So if everything pans, how it happens, that's why you guys are up there. You cannot govern in fear. When I say that is you cannot govern in fear of losing that seat. If you are for the people and if you're having conversations with the people, there'S No Way you're going to reach everybody. There'S No Way that you're going to reach everybody. Hear me clearly. You cannot good afternoon in fear. So if -- 13% of the City Of Tampa votes, so you want to put this on the ballot and always said, God, so many people are left out because the small amount of vote. So you want to put this on the ballot or the suggestion is for this to be put on the ballot for that small amount that's making the choice of who sits up there and who is mayor, they make the same decision about the rays. You as council members should be going out in the community and having conversations. If you are having conversation with vast amount of people that's not appearing here, then you're doing what you need to do. You're not going to reach everybody. You're not going to reach everybody. 11,900 jobs, the infrastructure, hell, even the Hcc, what it used to be called by HC. Again, there's bad in everything, but there is an outline of good. And we have to be patient enough for the good. I vote -- not I vote. I support yes on this if it pans out with the 11,900 jobs. The AMI in regards to the housing. That's what i've been fighting for all this time and what I support. Of course, the West Tampa Yellow Jackets. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. As I said, we're going to take a 15-minute break. It is 3:09. Let's be back in our seats at 3:25. 3:25. [ sounding gavel ] we're in recess. [Recess]
