segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Okay. Once again, we are doing public comment for joint Tampa City Council and CRA. That would be item 80 on the Tampa City Council agenda and item 1 on the CRA agenda. We left off with the wonderful Robin Lockett. We're going to move on. I'll call the next five names and see who will speak. By the way, nobody took me up on the you have to speak less than three minutes. We can always start new. Sierra Sizemore, Max Intridgo, sierra, come on up. Start with your name, please. Hi again. I would like to start by saying with gratitude saying i'm really proud of my community for coming out. The fact that there are so many of us here speaks volumes. I would like to thank you. I did come prepared with questions from my friends and community members and you guys asked very thought-provoking questions and answered all of those questions, at the same time, bringing in a bigger picture and showing more questions in the spirit of saying things that have not been said already, I have not heard very much mention of how this would affect high school students, hcc campus. I feel there is not enough funding to support kids as we're putting more and more expectations on them. Dual enrollment, virtual or in-person, i'm very worried about the transportation risk there with the bus route that was mentioned before. The businesses on Boyscout, I feel there's some concern with putting all of the funding towards fixing that specific part of dale mabry and Boyscout leading to the airport because most of the trouble on those streets is just outside that block. Just outside that block. And that's just directly the path from the airport to the stadium and all of those businesses on Boyscout are corporate. They don't support the local economy at all. They are half owned by Dardon. I just feel that's something to take into consideration for people who aren't here, can't reach everybody. I think we should consider the people affected day in and day out by the traffic routes and pedestrian concerns, just putting a few streets here and there. Boyscout also has the nicest streets i've seen in the majority of Tampa. Does not account for walkability the rest of dale mabry. Students that do this travel every day. I won't use my full time because i'm tired.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, sierra. Max Intridgo. Going once, going twice. Hi, max. My name is Max Intridgo. I also want to talk about the fact that as we've seen many times before, even in reports by the University of Denver Sports and Entertainment Law Journal, this will not actually revitalize our economy. It's been shown that when different stadiums enter, they promise higher consumer spending in local businesses, but that has been shown statistically to not have happened time and time again. They promise to bring jobs, but the jobs often go to transplants who end up moving here to take those jobs from the actual people who are here. It then also results in most of the money by the stadium that is earned by the stadium going to paying players who then return to their home cities, home states and spend it elsewhere. This money will not be helping our actual struggling citizens here as the rent crisis keep going up. This will not be helping us as our parents can't figure out a way to feed their children. This will not be Helping Any Way that actually matters to the citizens that are here and are asking for that help. We need to be actually doing things that are useful like subsidizing child care if we want to be introducing people to the workforce and introducing people into being able to spend more money on our local businesses. We need to be subsidizing bus transportation so people can travel to these local businesses. We need to actually be focusing on the people who are hurting and not on giving handouts to Large Corporations who already make billions. Thank you for your time.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for keeping it brief. Jason Hall. Chris. Jason Hall. Jason Hall. Not present. Chris. Come on up. Appreciate the time today. My name is Chris Bentivegna. This is definitely, you guys have a big decision ahead of you, right? Personally, when i'm faced with a big decision, I look back at what has happened in my past. There are similar type of engagements that you can look at? This is so big, I try to think about it, what has happened in Florida over the last x amount of years even close to this. Purely rhetorical question, 15 years ago, kind of a similarish type thing. If you think back 15 years ago, the whole high-speed rail project. The Citizens of Florida voted to have high-speed rail, connect Tampa to orlando. For whatever happened, for whatever reason, even though the citizens voted for it, that project didn't happen. So maybe it was the money involved was in the wrong political bucket. It didn't align with certain people's viewpoints and that'S Just The Way that project happened. What did we learn from that? Where are we at today? We have one of the most dangerous roads in the country connecting Tampa and orlando. We're nowhere close to having any other options to travel down that route. Decisions have repercussions, right? That is the large scale issue that we had there because we turned down that project. On a smaller scale, personal scale, my mom lives in south Florida, and she, it's much harder for her to visit her grandkids because there'S No Easy Way to get to Tampa. Elderly person being on an airplane is not the easiest thing in the world, even as a young person not that easy. As you consider this project, there's no perfect deal. There's just not. You can think about, hey, we'll make the deal perfect, go back and forth and negotiate things. It will never happen and you guys know that, right? This deal may not be perfect but it's pretty good. I say let's take this deal because it's not guaranteed this deal will be here tomorrow. It could go away. This is the opportunity now. Let's take this deal. Let's take Tampa and bring Tampa to the next level and make it that great city that we all know because we live here. Thanks, everybody.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, chris. Ray Wong. Devon Garrett. Elizabeth Braden, mr. Hayes. Hi, ray. It's been a little while since I was last year, and I think a lot has changed and a lot has been negotiated and deliberated and discussed. The one thing that has not changed is my belief this still represents a really great opportunity for the City Of Tampa. I'Ll Borrow Dr. Atwater's description and say that it really does feel like a generational opportunity, an opportunity that extends far beyond baseball, an opportunity to create jobs, attract investments, strengthen neighborhoods, improve infrastructure, and expand our tax base. Perhaps more importantly, it's an opportunity to continue Tampa's evolution into a truly great american city. We often talk about places like New York, chicago, san francisco, l.a., As cities that have shaped their own identities on the national and international stage. I believe that this is Tampa's moment and this is happening right now. Moments like this require us to think beyond the next election, the next budget cycle, and, yes, even as has been discussed today, the next decade or few decades. These moments require us to think about Tampa -- the Tampa that we want to leave behind for generations that follow us. There will always be reasons to be cautious. There will always be uncertainty surrounding something this ambitious. There are moments in history, in the history of a city when ITs leaders have an opportunity to do something brave, something visionary, something bigger than any one of us. I believe that this is one of those moments. I respectfully ask each of you to support this project and vote yes today. Thank you for your time, your leadership, and your service to our city.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, ray. Dayan Garnet, Elizabeth Brandon, Mr. Hayes, rachel. I would like to first start off with a picture right here that I put. This is the reason why i'm here in front of the council members today. This is my family story. I'm raising the next generation of Rays' fans. My son isn't even two years old. We watch the Rays together. If he doesn't fall asleep with his Rays' hat, he cries. Even when I take him to a game he'll sit still for SIX innings. Do you know how hard it is to have a two-year-old sit for SIX innings straight? SIX minutes he doesn't, but take him to a Rays' game he sits still. Vote no today, ultimately this team leaves Tampa Bay and I promise you I will bring him back down here and you will have to explain why his favorite baseball team is not here. The reality is there's no more time. Going on 20 times, it's time to bleep or get off the pot. The decision is about the next generation of Tampa Bay. If you want to be an oakland, ask them how redevelopment is going after losing their teams and their potholes got fixed magically. To those Planning no, let me let you in on a little secret. This ownership group could have bought the team and immediately started pitting cities against each other looking for the biggest handout possible. They didn't. They chose Tampa Bay. Started out with a 50-50 split. Now paying 60 percent. City ask was too high. You were brought into the negotiating room. We're talking about billion dollars of private investment. If you're voting no, tell me your alternative. Who is showing up tomorrow with billions of dollars to invest here? Because saying no is easy. Leadership requires having a better solution. And understand something else, if this fails, these owners will still be billionaires and other cities will want this team. To those voting yes today, thank you for having the vision to see what this can be and to the council members who disagreed at the beginning, I thank you for working through your differences and continuing to negotiate towards a solution. I'll leave you with this, years from now, nobody will remember the arguments made in this room, but my son may ask what happened to his baseball team and Tampa will remember who made that decision. Don't make the next generation of Rays' fans pay for a failure of leadership today. You're not going to please everyone. Think big picture. Think investment. Choose wisely, please vote yes.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, devon. Elizabeth, followed by Mr. Hayes and rachel. Good morning, start with your name, please. Hi. I'm Elizabeth Braden. I live in South Tampa. I'm asking you to vote no on the stadium. Three years ago, my daughter went to New College during the hostile take-over. Desantis put his cronies in charge, ballooned the expenses, and installed sports for the Students, this college didn't have sports before. The college rankings dropped. 30% of the faculty quit. A hundred Students transferred out. My daughter never finished her degree. I blame Desantis. The second hostile take-over is when New College took over USF manatee, 900 Students lost their campus. Now we have the third hostile take-over with Desantis and his campaign donors taking over Hillsborough College. Right now, the college only has $50 million to rebuild the campus. At the trustee meeting yesterday, the CFO said he needed an additional $165 million. How do you rebuild a campus when the funding is Not In Place and you don't have enough money? The state only promised an additional hundred million. Rays haven't signed up to give them any money. There's nothing in writing. Atwater says, yeah, we have a promise but, you know, you're going to have to fight for those funds and a lot of those funds are going to charter schools. You still haven't been able to fix your elevator. You capitulated as a group. You did not demand for the Rays to pay for the college and the Tax Office. You had that power. You still have the power now. They are demolishing eight buildings. Students will be in portables with messy and loud construction with No Place to park. Will they pay less in tuition? Probably not. Right now, the Students think that it's under renovation. They have no idea that things are going to be torn down, because of this upheaval, some courses will be discontinued. Students will drop out just like my daughter did. These kids won't be Able To Drive to ybor or brandon. And I think now that Atwater has said that I think we're only getting $150 million, I believe that this college will end up just being a shell of itself. So i'm asking you to vote no, because I think the value of a College Is Way better than a stadium.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, elizabeth. Mr. Hayes. Not here. Not present. Rachel Muscoso -- moscoso. Not present. We'll get done early like this. Carmen Edmonds, Kert Thoreson -- Carmen Edmonds is not in the room? Kert, come on up. Start with your name. Then enfant and who is this lena young green? Go ahead. My name is Kert Thoreson. There's been a lot of drama thrown around here. Democrat this, Republican that. People being accused of misogynistic things online. Accusation of paid actors downstairs. Fake college students. TSA members having their hands slapped -- getting kind of nasty. I came here back in May and I wore a Rays' polo. I corrected myself and said I was wearing a Tampa Bay polo. I grew up in this area. Raised manatee county. Here I am today in Tampa. Rays are my family in Tampa. My father used to take me to games when I was a child. And now, i'm doing the same. We're taking to the game on Saturday for a second birthday. I showed him a picture of a swimming pool and a picture of the baseball field. He ran towards the baseball field. This isn't just xs and os, isn't just dollar signs and cent signs. This is a community asset. I want to also show the sort of asset and philanthropic work that the Tampa Bay Rays engage in. Anybody willing to kiss this good-bye? I certainly hope not. There is recently a video posted on facebook about how the Arizona Coyotes and Kansas City Royals built multiuse districts and failed. Kansas city hasn't built anything yet. Arizona didn't build anything either and they didn't move. That is correct. They are in Utah now. Would you be willing to say good-bye to the Tampa Bay Lightning in a similar situation. Certainly hope not. Community asset. I've seen this tb in Tanzania, africa, Ecuador, Martinique, France, Germany, this is us. I don't see orlando hats. I don't see ocala hats. I don't see sarasota. This is Tampa and this is Tampa Bay. This is us. Finally, being involved with education myself, I know that it's a really big idea. The little boy, hope he goes to college, whatever -- in order to get into a really good school, you have to be dual enrolled. This county, the dual enrollment institution is Hillsborough College. It's not being abducted. It's not going away forever. It will be built better than ever and join us in the 21st century. Lastly, there was something mentioned earlier today and I want to go over this. I certainly did read the community benefits front to back. A lot of the asks that were mentioned, affordable and attainable housing, yes. AMI levels for students 80% and below, yes. Housing to live, work, and play in the community, yes. Quality in jobs, equitable living wage. Yes. Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. It was all there. Bit deceitful when people say it isn't. In case anybody wants to know --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: You are a teacher. See, you follow instructions well. [ laughter ] Marinella followed by Lena Young Green and Valerie Bullock and then Jp Peterson. Marinella Infante? Thank you for having us today. I'll try not to take three minutes. So many people have spoken before me and made very eloquent arguments on both sides, but I will say, would you jump into a pool without water? This is what this feels like. It feels like taking a chance on lack of transparency, unknown financials, documented studies showing proof of broken promises and failure, feels like a rushed job. Have to ask why. I think it's more important to let the voters understand what the final proposal is and let them vote on it rather than a small group of people doing this. I think we need more information about it. It just doesn't sound like a good plan. Like I said, other people have made very good arguments. I'm asking to you vote no on this.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. Lina. There you are. And then Valerie Bullock is going to be next and then Jp Peterson. Valerie Bullock in the batter's box. Start with your name, please. Thank you for the opportunity for us to come to speak to you today. I'm here supporting the correspondence that you received from our president and the presentation that he did before he left, representing Tampa Heights. For years and years, we've worked hard to ensure that Tampa Heights digs out of the doughnut hole that we've been in the middle of east and West Tampa, downtown, and Seminole Heights. As she shared, we believe that removing funds from the Downtown CRA will affect us in the progress that we are making. We also would like the expansion of our CRA, which is the smallest one, and would like to apply some of those to our housing issue. That would complement the fact that you approved a few years ago the overlay district of Tampa Heights to help ensure diversity and a mixed community in our Tampa Heights area. I also request that you consider in the community improvement component of this agreement that we think about the youth and the youth development as many of you have supported along with Tampa Heights Junior Civic Association. Thanks again for the opportunity.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Always lovely to see you. Valerie Bullock followed by Jp Peterson, Alison Hewitt and Elvis Piggott. I got to say that because I know a lot of people getting up here they are not even from the area. I was on a.i. Last night and I did an analysis of the battery which is in atlanta, and it said the tax revenue growth from the development, it said taxable property values in the district, it did jump from 5 million to 557 -- by 2024. Then I asked it what was the economic gains from it. But most of the economists, including JC Brad Bury from kenny saw state. Much of the spending shifts away from local businesses instead of creating brand-new economic activities. The cost to the taxpayer, critical studies estimate that public debt payments and operational costs leave a yearly shortfall of around 15 million, meaning the stadium project still places a financial burden on local taxpayers. The regional growth, it says, suggests that property value growth near the stadium matches normal regional trends rather than approving a special stadium bonus. I'm against this. The reason why i'm against it, they did extend East Tampa CRA, but with zero funding. We don't want an extension in years without the extension with the money. We need money. If you want to get serious about jackson heights, belmont heights and Sulphur Springs, you need the tax dollars over there, and that is not happening. Everywhere else places growth. I like the idea of extending East Tampa CRA because we've been fighting for it over 15 years. But it's useless to extend it and don't put no funding with it. And Sulphur Springs should have been included as part of the negotiating deal also. Sulphur Springs do not have a CRA. Downtown and on channelside, both of them CRAs need to be sunsetted because they don't need no more money. But we do need it in Sulphur Springs, and I don't like the idea because Sulphur Springs was left out. Really, you're not trying to help the slum and the blight. You're just doing East Tampa, symbolic. Another thing, the rays took the affordable housing out of the mixed use development. It will be mixed use development but no affordable housing. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Just for fyi, we have about -- if everybody takes all their time, we have 40 more minutes. Jp Peterson, Alison. Karen. Thank you, council for having us here again today on this historic day where the choice is clear. We can do something that provides the absolute gold standard for the public-private enterprise in building a stadium and vote yes or we can vote no and be chasing something like this for our entire lifetime. My worthy predecessor here talked about the atlanta battery. There I was when that whole thing went down. All the same arguments were made about it. And all the same economic studies were brought out. I, too, went on a.i. Last night, Dekalb County is making close to $11 million a year. Debt service is 6 million. Making plus, plus money on this deal for a long, long time. Turned a grove of trees into $40 million worth of tax revenue every year. And that's a proven model. That's what we want to do here. So all these economic videos that we're doing, using decades-old data are absolutely useless because this is the new trend in stadiums. This mixed use project and what the Rays are bringing here in $1.4 Million in investment, in just the stadium, how come nobody is talking about what they are bringing to the table. We're talking about what the public has. By the way, your contribution in the city is 3% of this deal. And you're getting 35% of the community benefits. I'D say that's a pretty good deal. I also want to talk about bringing us all together. I've been covering sports for 30 years in this market. I've watched the boat parades. Been there for the bucs super bowl. I've been there for the lightning winning two cups. Bringing people together in That Way is unlike anything we ever do. The civic pride that a baseball team brings is unlike anything that we can do in this city. I would tell you this, for all those people that don't want to give money to billionaires, i've got news for you, they'll take their money right Down The Road to orlando and they'll enjoy all the benefits while we Have To Drive i-4 to see the Rays play. More than anything, this is about visionary. This is about being visionary and showing leadership in this moment. We can nitpick all the little things in this bill and this isn't right, this isn't right, what if this happens, what if this doesn't happen, you will be paralyzed by inaction if this Is The Way you look at it. Paralysis by analysis. Make a bold choice today. Say yes, vote yes, and come party with us on the boat for the world series championship, Myself, Junior, jonathan, I think Mr. Babby will be there as well. And we can celebrate this as a community. Go Rays.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, jp. Allison, Elvis, Karen. Alison Hewitt, start with your name. You have three minutes. Alison Hewitt, third generation resident of East Tampa. I feel like i'm going to beat a dead horse here. Was feeling really happy, unfortunately, when the City Council was upset when they got the information last minute about the budget and had to make the decision. It's something, that especially in the East Tampa CRA, we've been begging to make sure that we have the information ahead of time so we're not coming here with motion. We're coming here with research and actual intelligent arguments for or against an issue. So I would like to ask to make sure the city attorney is able to state on the record whether the timing and manner of all the materials released satisfies the city's obligation under 286.011 And 286.0114 And any applicable city charter, ordinances, and the public right for meaningful participation. That was the first thing. The next thing on my issue is that several people have touched on, as you all know, East Tampa, third generation from East Tampa. We need to really make sure that we have an extension that's not just an extension in name only, and that the funds that are contributed by the county is very important. So that time, because East Tampa is finally moving forward, we have an incredible manager who is finally making sure that he is in the community talking to the community, making sure every step of the way we are doing progress. I want to also mention Drew Park. Been attending meetings there, as well as walking door to door with the chair of the CAC. We just need to make sure as we are so excited about a potential rays stadium that we do not dismiss the incredible Drew Park community, that we have anti-displacement plans put in there, not in the community benefits agreement but they should be. Need to make sure that we are making sure that the area that has been historically overlooked is now not completely beat down by thousand-pound giant that's coming in the area. Also make sure the housing, as we have seen, as we're doing affordable, attainable workforce housing around the city, we have given more funding towards the 80%. Real fight to make sure we have equitable funding for 30%. Make sure we keep an eye on that as well. The last thing is the CRA accountability. We need to make sure that as the funding is going through, that we are potentially create a dashboard like you did recently, be able to track the projects. We need to be able to track how this money goes as well. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Allison. Next speaker is Elvis, followed by Karen, Brett, Linda. I listened to the discussion. My story haven't changed. I think that it's very interesting, very nice. I want to most definitely give great respect and honor to the owner of the Rays. Ken Babby is phenomenal with just our conversations. My heart goes out. I listen and watch people put their kids up to watch the Rays' game. The Rays' stadium has made such a great impact with their kid's life. I want to talk about, when I talk about, what about our youth, our children, our tomorrow. The Rays know what they are going to get. Tampa know what they are going to get. But our young people, do they know what they going to get? We look and we look and I see that some of our kids, I was fortunate this year to take 46 kids over to the bucs' stadium when they had the back to school event. The only time they have been in the stadium is look in the stadium to get free book bags. To see what it looks like. I think at the end of the day, while we're talking about building a stadium, why that may be phenomenal why that may be nice, why that would be great. I would really like our youth to be the focus. When we talk about the future, we talk about our young people. We talk about the future, our young people are in trouble. I have a 33-year-old that is a single mother of four that just on Tuesday, her mom called me because she tried to commit suicide and take her own life. Her words after I got to the hospital was, life is hard. It's not the billionaire's fault that life is hard. It's nobody's responsibility to get our handouts. What i'm asking for and so grateful to God that somebody gave me an opportunity. Somebody gave me the exposure to see what else I can have in life. That's what shaped me to be who I am today. I'm asking that the Rays, i'm asking that Tampa, while we do this, wherever your vote goes today, that you also have the same passion, the same ambition and same determination to get security and secure our future. How, give them exposure, open doors and make sure that if this stadium is going to be built here, I hope and I will continue to work with Ken Babby to hope and have that opportunity that our young people right in East Tampa and not just Black, not White, i'm talking about our youth in general need the exposure to know we can't continue to watch hope sucked out of them. Our young people have lost the desire to dream. Let's bring it back. A lot of grown people come up here and celebrate how they can't wait until the Rays get here. Let's talk about our youth and make sure our youth is excited and protected and knowing that life is not over, that they, too, can go to Hcc and be successful. Drop-outs, young men trying to get a second chance in society. I would like to see this make a total round impact to Tampa and not just the ones that can afford it.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Thank you very much. Karen. Gary. Brett. Linda Taylor. Bob Morrison. I was not Planning on putting up my grandchildren, my two granddaughters. My daughter sent that to me today. They like ponies and unicorns. So i'm hoping that the city will consider funding their favorite recreational needs. I had to have my son pick up the daughter. Sometimes I help him pick up my five-year-old daughter from kindergarten because we need to make sure that she has good schools and good academics because she's going to be the one funding this. Thank you for giving three minutes. The County always cuts us off. I wanted to talk to you about the perspective of a business owner in Tampa. Seven years ago, my husband and I emptied our savings to buy property and start a business in Tampa. The city didn't give us the land. It didn't hand us the extra city property next door so that we could turn a bigger profit. The lot that we bought was suitable for what we wanted and not already serving the public as a college campus, a tax collector's office or a law enforcement headquarters. Our nest egg wasn't big enough to buy this property, so we had to refinance our home and take out another mortgage to buy the property. The city didn't chip in half. It doesn't tax our neighbors for 35 years to make our mortgage payments. When the roof goes, the city isn't coming to fix it. That's what the ordinary business owner gets. That's the treatment the ordinary business owner gets, and we work hard and we make it work. The rays are being offered something else. Public land, hundreds of millions of public dollars -- not hundreds of -- yeah, hundreds of millions of public dollars and decades of public financing around their private development. If we had been handed that kind of a deal, at least we would have given the public an ownership stake and a share in the revenues. I already pay twice as much in city property taxes as I pay on my home in the County. When City Hall is flush with cash, it finds money for the best connected partners. Ordinary taxpayers get the bill. Vote no on this. When amendment 3 is on the ballot, vote yes. Take the surplus away from municipalities that enable corrupt deals and allow it to stay instead in the people's pockets. The rush is telling. I just wanted to leave you, because I have extra time that i'm not used to getting with an aesop's fable. Sing now, dance now, Grasshopper said as the ant prepared for winter. Will we be ready when winter comes? Your vote today will tell us if you are an ant or a Grasshopper. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Thank you very much. Gary Dolgin. I'm Gary Dolgin like following karen, we were in home room in high school in 1982. I'm here as a citizen and as a huge Rays' fan. We're going into the bottom of the ninth inning now. Looks like it might be a one-vote margin here, just like the Rays have a one-run game. Maybe we ought to go to extra innings. Councilwoman Hurtak, I watched your video this morning. I was very impressed with it. It brought up excellent points. I think that any councilperson that votes yes on this today, I would like to hear them rebut her video. I want to thank Councilman Carlson for doing an excellent job of negotiating better terms, but I think the terms could even be better. I want to thank Councilman Miranda for 1996 when he voted no on the Bucs, and he has historical perspective here. But talk as a Rays' fan part of a season ticket group for years who has taken his son on Rays' road trips every year since he was nine years old and now 22, he called me from Washington today and said, dad, I really want this deal to go through. I said to him, I want to see it go through, too, but I want the Taxpayers to be protected. I said to him, you know, ari, you're still in school. You haven't graduated to being a full-fledged taxpayer yet. You might have a different perspective when you get a little older. What I would like to see is whenever you enter into a business deal, you're making a contribution. You're getting a stake. What about the Taxpayers having some type of equity interest so that you're guaranteed a rate of return? If the team makes a lot of money, how much is their value going to increase if this deal goes through? How much money are they going to make if the deal goes through? The Taxpayers should get a percentage of that. I want this deal to go through, but I want the Taxpayers to be protected. So I ask all of you who have had a very difficult decision to make, I probably have spoken with five of you. I appreciate the thoughtfulness that everyone had. Some people that are yes votes, some are no. Protect the Taxpayers. Let's get an even better deal than we have right now. If necessary, take it in extra innings and maybe we can have a walk-off with victory both for the city and for the Rays. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, gary. Brett followed by Linda Taylor, followed by Bob Morrison. Brett Gross. I've been covering this tiring stadium saga on youtube for the last ten years. The story has gone on a lot longer than just ten years. It's like a tv series where each season gets worse and more predictable. Rendering after rendering after proposal after proposal, but for the first time in this never-ending saga, it seems like we are actually getting there and closer than it has ever been. I live in wesley chapel. Takes a little over an hour every single weekday, the entire season. That's an issue with the entirety of pasco county and all the northern suburbs of Tampa. Having the stadium built would be very beneficial for the people of pasco county and suburbs as well that access the stadium. Let's not overlook the fact that with USF and ut students who already have to uber to Ybor City and soho for bars, it would give them a good option on weekends to just go out and have fun and have a place to go hang out. As USF alumni myself, I know I would have loved a place like this when I was a student. Point goes to show the different opportunities that the development would bring for those all around the region. Additionally, I was just in atlanta two weeks ago, the night life of the battery and the environment it creates for the fans and locals is truly remarkable. The entire time I was there, I was daydreaming about, that could be here. That could be Tampa. That could be our home as well. Imagine how much money in $20 beer sales alone you would get every single game and every bar outside of the stadium. It would be incredible. My final remark here will be if this fails to get approved and Rays end up leaving Tampa Bay entirely because of it, we lose this piece of our identity. The tb we wear on our hats, we lose this piece of our identity. Guarantees more people walking around Tampa in yankee hats. That cannot happen. Do the right thing. Vote yes on the stadium. Thank you very much for your time.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Brett. Linda Taylor and then bob. Linda Taylor? No. Bob. Then followed by steve. My name is Bob Morrison. I am here on behalf of the Hillsborough County Hotel and Lodging Association. In many ways, first, we appreciate what you've been going through because our industry has more than just a casual interest in this funding strategy. As you are well aware, over $300 million of tourist tax funds are part of the funding formula. Those funds only come from hotels. No local resident, no property owner, no individual taxpayer has a dime going into that pot. We've been doing the same analysis that you've been doing on the tourist tax side of the equation. We believe our conclusions have come to the following. Number one, we believe that anytime there's an opportunity to review a development that is going to take a hundred plus acres from non-revenue producing to revenue producing is worthy of your consideration. Secondly, we're also of the opinion that when we look at how to make this community, this community respond to the needs of job and job opportunities, we view this combination of stadium and multiuse as a difference maker. I was advised of something today that reinforced another key to our analysis. We did not want to see assets cannibalized. In other words, if you have something that already serves the market, let's not do something that just replicates. Well, I was advised today that the women's final four that has been a staple in this community, in many respects have helped to put them on the map as a go-to, be a part of event will no longer be able to be here in Tampa because our capacity at benchmark arena is not sufficient. Not enough seats. What the rays have done in redesigning the stadium for non-mlb events is where the economic development opportunity rests. We would urge you to give thought to that part of the equation because those -- that's where the delivery of the economic promise has the potential of Taking Place. Thank you for your time.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you very much. Steve, followed by, if justin hall is still in the room. Then Kella Mccaskill. Thank you for the opportunity to be here today. I'm Steve Cona. President and CEO of Associated Builders and Contractors, Florida Gulf Coast Chapter, representing 650 construction companies and thousands of skilled workers across the region. First, I just want to thank the City Council and the Tampa city team for the tremendous amount of work they have done getting us to this point. This is a huge economic development opportunity that could shape our region for the next two decades. From the construction industry's perspective and let me put that perspective into a Little Place here. We have 7% of our workforce in Hillsborough County is construction workers. Another 9%, close to 10% is construction related activities. We have seen a significant up-tick in companies investing in new workers in anticipation of this project. We get 2 to 20 calls a day with high school students coming, wanting to get into the construction trades, and that's because of the interest in projects like this. It's a significant uptick. We train all of our apprentices at our partner Hillsborough Community College. Longtime partnership with them, over 30 years. We're excited to be able to continue that partnership and train the best and brightest. Construction doesn't just build stadiums. It builds people. It creates long-term careers, and it grows small businesses. The apprentices that we train today become tomorrow's skilled craft professionals, superintendents, project managers, and many will eventually become owners of their own construction company. Imagine starting your career today as an Apprentice working on the new rays' stadium and being able to say the rest of your life "I built that." You guys have that opportunity today as well. That's the kind of opportunity a generational project can create. That is the legacy I hope we remember this project as it's considered. We encourage everyone to support this project. Thank you very much for your attention. Appreciate it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, steve. Again, for those in the back row, we can hear you. Please, if you want to have a -- and the front row. If you want to have a conversation, please take it out front. Kella, followed by Elijah and -- I want to start thanking you, being at the forefront of the project, from videos, keeping posts, keeping it educational for us in the community. Too often in years past, development happens to us. We're not as involved. We don't get to talk as much. They tell us what they are going to do in the community. Those of you that have done that, thank you. I want to also say This Is Way more complicated than something I can actually deal with. Somewhere between my City Council Shero and my City Council hero and the rest of you, i'm sure you'll figure it out. What I do know is that when channelside and Water Street received their money, I was reluctant coming from the West Tampa side. And I fell in love with the development once they broke ground, once they started, I saw what it could be. I've been there since 2013. I've learned to not speak prematurely. I can't see myself leaving. Been there ever since. I support this one of the things I love the most about this development is how we come down here and complain to you all as City Council members and we talk about what we want and what we don't want. We for years have asked, the last two years when they decided to strip CRA, we asked to extend ours before they do it. You heard that and you took that opportunity to get the other areas what they wanted. Heard Rick Fernandez come up and say, well, we need ours extended. If you were going to say yes to this, add the other communities and what they requested because the city was not interested in an extension. Probably not interested in extending boundaries. Use this as an opportunity to negotiate for some of the other areas. Now all of a sudden because they want this stadium, they'll listen to us and give us the other things we want. Lay it on thick. Add everything we want in this deal. I also want to thank for the Cba, I want to thank you all but I also want to thank the rays for letting me dump all the stuff that we don't get typically in a deal when it happens. When Water Street happened, we didn't get everything we wanted. Didn't even get to participate. He allowed us to share concerns outside of the deal. Concerns with the youth, met with the president, team, they are concerned with all the things beyond what is on the Cba agreement. I want to thank them for being very forthcoming, sitting down listening to me. You know how I can get. Listening to me and all the things I wanted to share. I appreciate that. While this is a very complicated decision, it's in your hands. I support what you all come up with. I hope they continue to do what they have been doing. They have been in the community talking to people, asking what we wanted. Wrote it down, reshared it, put the information. I have no doubt they'll do what is right on that end in addition to the agreement. I want to make sure you do the same. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Kella. Elijah Fluellen in the room? Very good. Start with your name, please. I come before you today to say the Rays' stadium project could be monumental for the region, allows unlimited opportunities to be something. Tampa Bay area that we love to call home. Love this area and this baseball team far too much to not speak my piece for this wonderful development to witness it first hand both on the business and entertainment side to tell you that this is the group to lead the charge for the next generation of scholars, dreamers, doers, and Rays' fans at the corner of north dale mabry and West Tampa Bay Boulevard. I turned 30 last Friday. People have been asking me since middle school where the Rays' are going to play next. I hope with today's vote we get more clarity as to where and when. I'll close with this. There is a whole stable of supporters around the Tampa Bay area and beyond that are ready to support this ballpark development. Thank you for your time and work. God bless, and raise up.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. The remaining speakers, Brandon Barclay, Andy Scaglione, Jamie Swift -- council, as you know, I meet with dozens and dozens of organizations every year. I'm told promises from all these organizations, all these politicians. We reached out to the Rays. We told them what our concerns were from a public safety standpoint. They addressed each and every one of those through multiple meetings. If you have a no vote on council today because you individually have a problem with the Rays, the problem lies with you. You are the elected officials. You are the people who are supposed to be reaching out, voicing your concerns on behalf of the public. You tell them what the concerns are and they either comply and address the concerns or they don't. If you have concerns today that are unaddressed, you have nobody to blame but yourselves. I'm asking for a vote in favor of this today. Again, we've spoken with fire, and i'm not going to speak on their behalf. I know Mr. Babby addressed my concerns. I know he addressed fire's concerns about all kinds of issues, about structural issues, transportation issues. Obviously, everybody here sitting behind me that is Westshore Alliance, Hillsborough College, they all came out and voiced this opinion. You've had months and months to state your concerns to the Rays. If you still don't have an answer, then i'm hoping you're willing to publicly say today when you vote no, this is the reason why I personally voted no on it. What is the exact reason and were they given the opportunity to address that. If the answer is no, it's all smoke and mirrors. Again, I come from a profession where we have to make life-and-death decisions in a split second. To say we need more time on this is laughable. I've been at least three meetings going on 30 hours of just chewing over the same thing over and over and over. Please get to a vote. Please do it quickly. Everybody here would like to go home.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, mr. President. Andy Scaglione followed by Susan Swift. Is susan in the audience? She left. Okay. Actually, i'm really excited. Andy Joe Scaglione. Again, i'm really excited about the rays coming to Tampa. I grew up in West Tampa. Played baseball most of my life in West Tampa Little League. I'm really happy and appreciate that you all, the CIT is not being used for part of this. You all kept your word with the voters which is very important, unlike our friends in the county. I knew -- I kind of felt good about it when I saw the letter written on June 4, 2024 and I saw the signature behind it was John Bennett. With his integrity, I knew it would work out. He would do the right thing. I do have a problem with the incremental dedication schedule with no assurances on the development timeline. And also the TIF provision, which is actually a rebate. None of us in this audience, when we pay our properties get a rebate at the end of the year for what we paid. In essence, we're paying with our own dollars. Most pro formas i've reviewed probably in my 41 years in business, probably over a thousand pro formas. I can say this. Most of them are wrong. Without crawl-backs or assurances, don't go on pro formas. You will be disappointed. There was a council member that put out a post last night that said 62.9% Private, 37.1% Public. Actually, that's not correct. When you include the $300 million of interest that nobody talks about regarding the TDT tourist tax, and you put in the land, those ratios aren't correct. Main thing i'm very disappointed about is the community benefit agreement that came out 36 hours ago. On March 10, 2026, we were all, Councilwoman Young, Miranda, two county commissioners, Harry Cohen and Myers, we were at the Jefferson high school. And we were assured by the rays, Mr. Babby, that there would be a much affordable housing at the district baseball area and mainly because those people are going to work there and Ms. Naya wanted a live, work, play environment. So far I have not seen that. We need to really work on this. Once you vote on this, this is a binding agreement. You have no leverage. I'm relying on you all to delay this until you get this settled and this is really, really important for the people that can't speak for their self that need this affordable housing very much. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Jamie Jones? Jamie Jones in the house? Jade Scott? Jade Scott? No. Okay. We've got Jamie Jones and then Fran Tate is going to close us out. Oh, Michael Randolph online. Andy. [ sounding gavel ] neighborhood association. I'm an urban planner. Run a civil team. Ya-da ya-da. Professional credentials. These are the things that I think haven't been said so I don't repeat everyone else. West Tampa Heights won't hate you guys about the outcome of this vote. We're going to respond about what happens after, right? Really, it's your successors who will have to deal with this and the taxpayers for 65 or 35 years, like everyone has already said. I am disappointed that there's no community benefits agreement being voted on at the same time. I have extremely low confidence in the community benefits agreement being enforceable without being part of this current vote. At the very least, I thought that Councilwoman Young would get a carve-out of affordable housing. Some of this donated land should surely be donated straight to the Tampa Housing Authority. This development is Not Water Street. This isn't downtown. My area is low density, low income, lower income, and has a very suburban roadway infrastructure. That's going to make things difficult to get out what you think you're going to get out of it. No one is talking about what happens immediately after this deal is approved. No one has explained what has to happen to help the rays build as much as possible as quickly as possible. I wish everyone could be clear that the goal here would be to minimize the amount of land dedicated to cars and maximize the amount of land that goes to sales tax generating retail and commercial uses, cutting out so many things about education and very, very localized benefits that need to be part of this. The residents and business owners around this development should be scared sh-tless at the words, build as much as possible as quickly as possible. Best case, the city will be forced to upzone our area to bring in more people to patronize the businesses that we intend to build or at least the retail spaces that we intend to build, and also best case the city will be forced to invest in transit so people can get to our area without driving. Otherwise, our area will continue to be parking lots. Parking lots, parking lots. That's it. And then the last thing i'll say is, i'm scared about the US. Bond market right now. I hope everyone else is paying attention to that. It is your responsibility to make sure that the US. Manages our debt Load The Way it should. I know we are a little part of the US. But still. Thank you, everyone.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Fran Tate followed by Michael Randolph. I am Fran Tate. 21-year community leader of East Tampa, member of the East Tampa community advisory committee of the East Tampa CRA. Four years. Transparency, accountability, experience, wisdom, knowledge, understanding. As you requested, chair Clendenin, I won't repeat the words of Reverend Dr. Jeffrey Johnston, lieutenant united states navy. I won't repeat the words of Ms. Valerie Bullock, community member of East Tampa. I won't repeat the words of Ms. Alison Hewitt, East Tampa resident. I'm just going to say i'm in agreement with everything each one of them said. Remember, 2044, 2044 as it relates to the East Tampa CRA. 2044. Little bit disappointed that Sulphur Springs was not included in this deal, in this discussion. Thank you all so very much for your hard work. We know you're going to do the right thing. God bless all of you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Fran. Michael Randolph, you are our last public speaker today. Bring it home. Thank you very much. My name is Michael Randolph with the West Tampa CDC. Let me start off by saying that we do support in theory and in concept the deal that's before us. The final deal will get a hard yes from us once the numbers worked out. City has got these type of deals right, three things in common. A fixed dollar figure, hard percent set-aside and public body that keeps check after the ribbon ceremony is all over. Starting with the strongest examples, the -- west end deal totaled about $600 million, specific number rather than goals. In that deal, they committed 100,000 a year for youth soccer, 100,000 for housing needs and $25 an hour minimum wage for workers as well as 25% set aside for minority business. Columbus went even further, committing over 50 million with a firm 20% of affordable housing units requirement built into 855 unit development near the stadium. Buffalo bills deal is the strongest model for ongoing accountability. Instead of one lump sum commitment, it created a Community Benefit Oversight Committee that meets monthly in public, tracking workforce diversity, living wage, diversity, food insecurity and education. This oversight structure is one that we need for Tampa. The centerpiece of this proposal is to community benefit agreement. Immediately binding commitment of this kind established in West Tampa as part of the rome yard project. A two-part agreement. One part for the city and one part for the West Tampa CDC. Under the agreement, we receive an office and training center for the West Tampa technology, wealth building and job creation center, the creation of 80 a.i. Resident owned businesses and up to 30 home-based businesses with -- financing to provide capital to the so-called -- in dei. Mei, that is -- first of ITs kind combining community development, entrepreneurship, artificial intelligence, and technology --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, michael.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Mr. Randolph. Your time has expired, my friend. Thank you for sticking with us all day. That concludes public comment. This is now an opportunity for Council Members to pontificate.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Can you tell us what the process will be now?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: This is what the process is. We'll go through, this is the council's opportunity, one at a time, we'll go through and you can say what you have to say. If you still have any questions, although we passed that period -- why do we have the feedback on the mikes? It's weird. If you have any questions, and if the staff is still available, I don't see any reason why you shouldn't be able to have that opportunity. Try to keep it contained and not repeat ourselves. This is the opportunity, as I told Councilman Miranda earlier today, it wasn't the time to pontificate, but now is your time. I have a statement i'm going to read. That's all i'm going to do.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: We're not going to convince each other to change our minds. If we could each take two rounds max and not spend --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I think that is a wise decision. I'm going to take one round. I'll start unless somebody else wants to. Councilwoman Young, go ahead.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Thank you. Attorney Shepard, are you on?

segments.speaker: Cliff Shepard
segments.text: Yes, i'm on.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Thank you for sticking with us. I have a question. It was brought up a few times during the public comment regarding the CRA extensions, particularly with the county not contributing to the CRA. Could you speak about that, please?

segments.speaker: Cliff Shepard
segments.text: I can speak about it with the caveat that I have not discussed any of this with the county and going totally off the paper. Unfortunately as some of you know and maybe some of you don't, paper changed from this morning at 8 something in the morning till last night when I sent you with the memo with the draft I had been given at 6:32 p.m. In the original papers I sent last night -- can you all hear me?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Little bit of reverberation.

segments.text: Could you speak a little more into the microphone?

segments.text: Is this any better? If not, I can change to a different device.

segments.text: Are you in a room with an echo?

segments.speaker: Cliff Shepard
segments.text: No, i'm in the same room i'm always in. I can try to call in from my phone if that helps.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: County Attorney. Sorry, I was just coming back over when I heard there was an issue. Let me make sure I characterize what your question is, Councilwoman, so that I can properly have that conversation with the County Administration because i'm going to need to get back with them and we'll get an answer very quickly here. What I understand your concern is it only relates I think to the East Tampa CRA, is that correct?

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: I'm seeing right here it says the County will not appropriate or pay any increment to the redevelopment trust fund for each such community redevelopment area, and then it was brought up about three times during public comment that the County would not be contributing to the CRA's past the sunset deadline.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: Right now, the way it works, and you probably all know this, again, i'm trying to catch up to where we are right now. We have specific end dates for all of the CRAs. For example, West Tampa I think 2043. I think East Tampa is 2034.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Attorney Shepard, you have to mute yourself, please.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: What we were willing to put into this initial conversation, because keep in mind, you still have a lot of steps you need to take to get there the county would agree to the extension, which we might not agree or we might not agree anyway, we're agreeing now to the extension, but we're not agreeing to put in any increment. Doesn't mean during the process conversation can't happen, but as we stand right here, we're not agreeing to put in for those extensions any increment. I think we need to all understand that going through a process of extension would Be Taking Place on each one of these. We're just having that conversation now versus having that conversation later. And as we stand right now, those are the ones that we're saying, we're fine if you want to go ahead and extend them. But the county is not willing to put in any of ITs increment for that extension. Again, we would still have an opportunity to have that conversation through an entire separate process, sort of previewing where we live right now. The only thing I can do if we want to have a different conversation is talk to the county administrator and see, that's why I just wanted to make sure I understood, are we talking about East Tampa? I think we are agreeing to some increment on the extension of Drew Park, but East Tampa, we did discuss West Tampa, but we went ahead and took out the extension on that. That goes until 2043. There is a lot of time to have those conversations and have that thoughtfulness. I just want to make sure I understand where your issue is so I can properly ask the question.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: How much does the County contribute?

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: East Tampa.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: That's a question i'll need to get information on. I simply do not have it as I sit here. If you want me to convey to the county administrator is that question, how much is it, and where she stands on that, i'm happy to do that. It would take me a few minutes to get the information.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Director McCray, I think he would know the answer to that question.

segments.speaker: Cedric McCray
segments.text: Tampa CRA director. Currently, the county contribution is 80% to the East Tampa TIF.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: 80% of their TIF. [Indiscernible]

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: There are two separate ones. The city and the County. City gives a hundred percent. The County gives 80%. And now they would be giving nothing.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: That conversation would have to happen on any extension. Two pieces of this. One, whether or not the county is agreeing to the extension. Two, whether or not the county is going to provide any of ITs increment. Even if you do nothing today and it's silent on those issues and we aren't having that conversation, there has to be a conversation at some point in the future to allow for those extensions. So we're just previewing that right now where the county is, but like I said, I can get in touch with the county administrator and see if there's someplace else that she can go on that. Keep in mind, she'd have to run numbers. It would be hard for her to figure that out at this moment. She probably can. She's good at math and i'm not good with math. Why don't I go and have that conversation with her and you can -- you guys, apologize, you all can continue your deliberation and see where you are.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, ms. Mandell. Councilman Carlson and Councilwoman Hurtak.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson

segments.speaker: Cedric McCray

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: What the county is saying is that they are okay sticking to this deal until it would have normally ended. So, like in East Tampa, 2034, whatever it was, they are okay keeping with whatever they promised here. Just the part after that. And if Chair Young would like to make a motion to get that forward on the East Tampa, happy to support it and see if the county would support it. What I would like to do is just respond to a few things mentioned in public comment and then make a statement in the second round.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Perfectly appropriate.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I said this before but several people mentioned amendment 3. This land has no property taxes on it right now. So even when we talk about the tax revenue sharing in the future, there's no property taxes today. So we don't put in the $80 million loan, there's no money to take back anyway. That's our choice. Do we want it or not? But there's no base. There's most likely no homesteaded property, so there's no taxes come in and go away. The big challenge would be the slowed growth of the commercial property from 10% to 5%. But we're not taking the 80 million as a loan. Before it was CIT and would have been taking out of fire trucks and police cars, we're not doing that now. Big reduction on the city side, we won't have taken more money, in fact, after ten years we'll have money that we'll be able to put back. Several people mentioned economic impact. I don't believe in economic impact numbers either. As I said earlier, people that pay for positive impact numbers and people that pay for negative economic impact numbers. I don't believe either one of them. Gone through both of them. They are both biased by the models they put together. Why is it that Republicans and Democrats can go through the same math and come back with different answers. It's because of the different perspectives they have. It's not just the math. There's not a single answer to these things. Also, some folks mentioned the TIF and Cdd and about transparency, the reason the TIF and the Cdd are there is for transparency. Because what other deals have done in the past is they have given money to a developer and then you don't have public insight into it at all. None of the money from the city is going to the rays. None going to the rays. Cdd, community development district that would be reviewed by the public. You will be able to pull public records whenever you want. Sit in the meetings, and the money is restricted that it can only go to public sector infrastructure that would be owned by the city, county, or state, just like the straz center, for example. It's owned by the city. They make improvements on it, we still own it. Talked about East Tampa, East Tampa is still going to have whatever city money is promised All The Way through. Nobody is taking away the city money. City will still pay 100% All The Way through the extension. The only question is the county, not the city's contribution. So that's all I have right now.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilwoman Hurtak followed by Councilman Viera and then Councilman Miranda.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I mean will be provided. Just a nice simple sentence added to that. It's going to be in the operations agreement, which will be with the county. It's not going to be with us.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: If there's no amount listed, I understand that the County, you said earlier that the County is the one that's going to argue over that. But I don't want that space left blank if this moves forward. So i'm going to recommend no less than $75 million.

segments.text: I'll just throw that out there as my suggestion. I just don't think we should leave that blank. Could be $10,000. Those are my only questions and stuff around that. That's it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: General statements permissible at this time?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you very much. I've spoken a lot on this before at prior meetings. I wanted to address some points. I always say this a lot in City Council because I said it for 20 years in my cases in litigation, there are a lot of things in life Black and White, right and wrong and many things that have gray. I think it's important that when you are arguing for something to acknowledge the gray and acknowledge the detriment something has even if you support something. First, you start off with a proposition. The idea this is probably the biggest vote we'll take up as elected officials. Councilman Miranda may have had a couple of others throughout his time, but you have to acknowledge the good as well as the bad. For me, reasons that i'll explain, I think the good far outweighs the bad. I'll talk about both. I think you have to be transparent. First off, when you talk about the changes, I think it's important for me this sort of talks about why -- i'll talk about my own vote. Voted to keep this alive. Voted to not walk away. The issue wasn't married to a particular set of terms that were on the table. Walk away and end discussions. That was it. I think that the improvements we've seen and i'll talk about some of those things that I think are very commendable, I think, are supportive of that vote. There are a lot of good things we should be celebrating and talking about here. Number one, for a stadium deal of almost $2.4 Billion, this is something pretty fiscally sound. Almost two-thirds, about 63% of this is going to be from the private sector. I know there's been some discussions on that in public comment. That's a pretty big success. Loan paid off from revenue from the project. You're going to be talking about the community benefits agreement, something that we're going to be dealing with if this goes forward, that's going to have a lot of advancements for the community. Councilwoman Young talked about a lot of issues close to my heart. This is our big chance to effect change on issues involving mobility, public safety, youth empowerment, apprenticeships and so forth, other things. Some of the CRA changes that have been proposed, Councilman Carlson I think has done a great job on a number of issues, including that. You take a look at the fact that Drew Park is protected. That's something that's very important. I'll talk about Drew Park briefly in a little bit. East Tampa expanded. The Downtown Tampa CRA being capped. We've heard about that. I always support it. Councilman Carlson always LED on that. Always supported his efforts. I think that's something so important. I've been passionate about the fact that I voted against big projects in the Downtown CRA because I don't think they pass the muster test on whether or not we would have spent it in downtown as opposed to other parts of the city. Downtown CRA still going to have money. If there are parts of northern downtown still blighted, then let's spend it over there. But capping it is just common sense, and that's something aside from this deal that should happen but something that's going to support this deal. This is a good deal for the City Of Tampa. You've got about three-quarters of a million dollars coming from Hillsborough County, about a -- strike that, a billion dollars, coming from Hillsborough County. About a quarter of a billion dollars coming from the State of Florida, all spent within city limits. All within city limits for this development and our ask is something that comparatively speaking about three to four percent of the total project is less than mod nest comparison. This process has been extremely inclusive. When the rays first came and talked about an April deadline, I said that will never happen. April, may that will never happen. I would never support that. What we've seen has been something very inclusive. We saw Mr. Brandon Barclay from Tampa Police Benevolent Association. We heard from firefighters. As Mr. Stocco said with Tampa firefighters, first responders have been given a place at the table to be heard. They have been given a place at the table. That's something very important. They met with, we saw Mr. Cona here from abc. They have met with the central labor committee. Local afl-cio and with the Skilled Trades Community and we're also working on meetings with HART, if this is something that should go forward. So public safety has been given a very big priority with a perspective move of district one from ITs location now into this development, having a Tampa fire station, substation preference in this development, we cannot repeat the mistakes of the past that we've done. You know what, i'll finish my other remarks in my second round.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Miranda.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Thank you, chair. I sit in the middle of this. To my west is Drew Park. To my east is the neighborhood of west -- both are going to suffer. Drew Park has been working and getting it done, and now that they have an opportunity to get income, no good for us anymore. We're going to take over that land and be something else. What a country. That's what divides a country, not unites a country. When you look at the things and say how does this happen? It happens because we let it happen, not because we want it to happen. The elected official's responsibility to do an act as you see it best for the City Of Tampa, not for myself or yourself. So all these things are going on. Did they meet with everyone? Damn right, I would have done the same thing, too, if I want to do something right. I admire Mr. Baker for doing what he did. However, when you look at this, Drew Park is there waiting to be something better and now we cut them out and say you're no good for us anymore. You figure it out. Who is going to get the traffic? Anyone here is going to get the traffic on the board here today, more than likely not. But Drew Park is going to be inundated with traffic. There are not 12 games or 15 games like at rays' stadium -- I mean the bucs stadium. There's 81 home games. Some are at night. Some are during the day, and they are going to be inundated between that and the other side and the concerts. How much is this neighborhood going to be able to hold and they get zapo for it. The big guys are coming in. I'm not against anything. But when I look at this, how would you feel if you lived in Drew Park or lived in West Tampa? I don't see anybody say i'm happy in the audience. They get nothing, nada. Zero for what they have done for this city. And i'm going to sit here and listen to this? What is a cdd? Can anybody tell me? Tell me what a cdd does.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Community Development District. Usually used to build out infrastructure and usually it's used in green field areas but we also used it at least in one case in the urban area. In this case, it's being used to be a pass-through for the funding to pay for the infrastructure that will then be owned by the community, but it's a government entity that is subject to public records and sunshine.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: I was raised in Ybor City. I have a different opinion. Getting paid with your own money. Washing the money and giving you your money back. That's what it is. It makes no difference to me what I say because what I say is what I mean, exactly what I say. If it was a regular deal, like Westshore is going to be. Midtown pays $8 million a year in taxes. This is altogether different. It goes into the Cdd and they give you the money back to you that you are supposed to get in taxes as payment. There is a difference to some degree. If i'm wrong, please correct me. I guess i'm right. No correction. So what am I doing here? Who is benefiting from this? Not the people in Drew Park. Not the people in West Tampa. That's all i'm going to say. Thank you.

segments.text: Thank you. Councilman Maniscalco.

segments.text: Thank you very much. In regards to the community benefits agreement, it was released Tuesday night. A very lengthy list. How enforceable is that, Mr. Steady? Since it's not in the document, does this have to go through the county and in the future it comes back to us?

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: We haven't agreed to it. It's not negotiable. What needs to happen is we need to negotiate a community benefits agreement. That's just their proposal as far as i'm concerned. It is, it's their proposal. Once the number is established, we get 35%, we need to come back with a community benefits agreement. We need to negotiate it.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: And then can we, when we say negotiate, can we say we want to allocate hundred percent to this or 25% to this, whatever -- customize as we wish.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
