segments.text: Okay. We talked about the CIT. I talked about the CIT. We talked about amendment 3. Amendment 3 is very dangerous because what's coming on the ballot should it pass could be catastrophic. It will be $35 million the first year off the city. At the county level it's in the hundreds of millions of dollars, from my understanding. And in that, since this is a multi-jurisdiction agreement, CIT is being used, not here but over there. And the hits of what amendment 3 does in the loss of revenue is very significant. I'm concerned, not that i'm against this development. I wish that the timing was different because we don't know what's coming. A storm that's coming that it may not even pass. It needs 60%. The hit that we get as a municipality and as a county and as a state is going to be catastrophic. Those are the words that i've seen. Those are the words i've heard. Dangerous, catastrophic. So I have a lot of concerns. I commend the organization for all their work because they have really been out there. They have met with everybody. They talked with everybody, or almost everybody, and they have made a lot of changes from may until today. But I just have this concern of what's going to happen in November, and it's going to be a significant amount of damage that comes to us and to all those around us should it pass. That's it for now. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Okay. I'm going to use my time to make basically my statement of position. I think we've kind of beaten a dead horse. Let me begin by stating i've supported this project since the memorandum of understanding. My support has been consistent, public and deliberate because I believed from the beginning that this new Rays ballpark together with the development around it presents a significant opportunity for Tampa. But support was not a surrender. Supporting the project was never meant giving anyone a free pass. It has never meant abandoning scrutiny, accepting weak terms or placing the interest of private organizations ahead of the people that we represent. We asked very difficult questions. We examined the numbers, we pressed for strong protections, we negotiated improvements, and we insisted that the agreement deliver meaningful value for Tampa. That work made this proposal stronger. I also want to recognize those that helped make this possible. First, Councilwoman Naya Young. She was one of the early supporters of making sure that we extended the East Tampa CRA. She was one of the first persons that came out swinging about jobs. She brought that to the table from the very beginning in the negotiations. Councilman Viera, Councilman Viera came out strong swinging for folks with disabilities, which he always does. He came out strong for first responders, our fire and police and he worked with the Rays' organization to ensure all of those groups were protected in this agreement and which also makes the City Of Tampa stronger. And then lastly, Councilman Carlson, a lot of what we see here is we have now been able to rely on Councilman Carlson's business acumen. He was able to identify areas in this agreement that could be improved because he understood the business and mechanics of it. He was able to take the agreement from an agreement not incentivized to an agreement that was incentivized for development. A lot of folks talk about how the thing would be built out. The agreement negotiated is an improved agreement because they will have incentive to build it out. I also want to acknowledge our partners at Hillsborough County Commission, particularly Commissioner Ken Hagan in his 20-year quest to retain major league baseball in the Tampa Bay area and the city and county staff reviewed the legal, financial, and operational details of this agreement. Their work helped protect the public interest and improve the proposal that is before us. After that work, I believe the conclusion is clear. This agreement deserves our support. I'm supporting it because I believe it is -- it is in Tampa's best long-term interest. It is not merely a vote on a baseball stadium. It is a vote on whether Tampa is prepared to compete for investments, jobs, housing, education, and opportunity or whether we're willing to let those opportunities go elsewhere. The final project is approximately $2.36 Billion. The Rays' ownership group is committing approximately 1.37 Billion, accepting responsibility for all the cost overruns, the city contribution is capped at $80 million. Those facts matter. We're not writing the check -- the Rays a blank check. We're not agreeing to cover cost overruns. We're not assuming responsibility for construction defects. We're not committing to unlimited public funds without conditions, oversight or accountability. The public contribution is capped. The private investment is substantial. Public dollars are subject to protections before they can be deployed. I want to say that again. The public dollars are subject to protections before they can be deployed. That's not an open-ended giveaway. It is a negotiated public-private investment with defined limits and public safeguards. The stadium is only part of the opportunity. The larger opportunity is the district around it. A connected, walkable, mixed use neighborhood with housing, restaurants, retail, hotels, public spaces, transportation improvements and a reimagined Hillsborough college. The Rays have also committed to a much larger privately financed development around the stadium creating the potential for billions of dollars in additional private investment. All within the City Of Tampa. That could mean construction jobs, permanent jobs, new businesses, new housing, expanded educational opportunities, and a stronger tax base to help support the services Tampa residents expect and deserve. Now let us address the questions that matter most to taxpayers. What does this agreement mean for Tampa taxpayers? It means the final agreement is materially better than the structure contemplated in the original MOU. The earlier proposal involving the city's community investment tax and the hundred million dollars CRA contribution, it's no longer in the structure before us. Do you mind if I finish this?

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Time it up like you tell me. [ laughter ]

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I'll do exactly what I tell Charlie Miranda. You're out of order. I'll finish my statement in the second round. Go ahead.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Ms. Scharf, this is a bombardier global 7500. When it was delivered to ITs owner three years ago, it was the largest and fastest civilian jet in the world. Only Concord was ever faster. List price starts at $80 million and it costs 4 million a year in operating expenses. It is the primary duty of every legislative body to identify the problems facing their constituents, identify the cause of those problems, and to address those causes by responsibly appropriating money to eliminate those causes. That was true when Aristotle wrote it 2300 years ago and it's true today. Which of Tampa's problems is being solved by committing $120 million to a baseball stadium? It's not 80. It's 120. We still have to pay the interest. We were elected to solve problems, not create new ones. Like those which will result from us having to borrow money at the worst possible time interest rate-wise from canceling planned infrastructure repairs, and that's before the specter of a property tax amendment passing. A comprehensive survey of 120 studies over the last 30 years in the Journal of Economic Surveys came to the following three conclusions: one, the deep agreement and research and findings demonstrates that sports venues are not an appropriate channel for local economic development policy. Two, even where positive relationships exist, estimated benefits tend to be insufficient to justify the level of subsidies provided. Three, despite this consensus findings of economic studies that the benefits of hosting professional sports franchises are not sufficient to subsidize public subsidies, taxpayer funding for the subsidies continues to grow. We have decades of research showing how and why these projects don't create jobs and don't create a significant or sustainable economic boost. The deal currently on the table is a bad one for Tampa taxpayers and workers. The seven of us today have a fiduciary duty to make wise choices with every tampe o's tax dollar. The question today is, will the seven of us recognize that we are ethically and morally obligated to start over and find a better deal for the city we represent and ITs citizens? Now is the time to prove that Tampa is the smart city. Tampa is the one that finally said no to the surge of forcing taxpayers to subsidize billionaire team owners. I am not anti-stadium. I guarantee you if we find a better solution, i'll be at more games than anyone else in this room. Consider that it is currently also a blank check to the rays to maintain and repair the stadium, because it's not that -- that sentence isn't in there yet that Tampe Os are expected to put up this money, won't have ownership share, all control of land development to the county even though literally in Tampa. This is a bombardier global 7500. When it was delivered to ITs zone, Patrick Zalupski. He paid $800 million for it. He spends $4 million a year operating it. Now he says he needs $80 million from us?

segments.text: Councilman Miranda.

segments.text: I listened very carefully. When you look around and you say, well, we'll get development, from 1996, tell me what new development came in some corner on MLK and dale mabry. I've just never seen it. So what am I doing here? How can you do this alone in a way? How can you vote on something you don't even know what's going on? All the papers coming in, didn't see until Monday afternoon and then changes made. What business acumen, who would you hire to do the job and not look at what the hell looking at to make a decision. segments.text: I'm not going to use my time but correct a couple of things. One, you refer to this in a way that the evidence submitted today does not substantiate. $80 million that we're borrowing is paid for by TIF return that only materializes if this construction project moves forward. That money does not exist unless this construction project moves forward. It is money that is created by the project that's going to repay the city the money we're taking out. So that is a wash. On the fire station thing, I think that is an inaccurate assertion. Paid $24 million for the last fire station. Your math don't add up. On the guarantees, there are so many guarantees in this 140 plus page document and everything is linked, if you read the document, truly read the document, you'll see that everything is backstopped for the city specifically. There are backstops in every part of that agreement. If we don't reach an agreement on a community benefits agreement, no money is transferred. If we don't do this, no money is transferred. Don't do that, no money transferred. Our City Staff and the County Staff and the county administrator have done such a tremendous job negotiating this agreement, I cannot tell you how impressed I am, including with the changes that Councilman Carlson brought forth to make this a better deal. I thought the deal we had when we did the MOU was a good deal. We've got a great deal now. We are so protected. I don't think there is a city in the United States of America that has been building professional sports that would not die for this agreement, there are cities all over the country bending over backwards, talk to jacksonville about how much money they are spending on their stadium. Talk to Kansas city, talk to las vegas, talk to anybody. Spending fortunes. And we have a private company that's coming in with over a billion dollars, 1.37, Something like that, billion dollars of private money just for the stadium construction, not to mention the billions of dollars of adjacent construction around that with the hotels and apartments and restaurants and all that. All of our money, our negotiators, our City Staff that we love and trust, they negotiated a deal with these private people that we're only spending it on the stuff horizontal, nothing vertical. It's the ditches. It's the sewer pipes, water pipes, streets, sidewalks. It's the stuff the city is supposed to be doing. I really applaud our City Staff for doing what they did. Because I went off on a rail, if you would like to respond, I would welcome your response. Sorry about that. Who is next?

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Thank you very much. So I have spent a lot of time with these documents. A lot of time. I have read a lot. I've asked a lot of questions. I read even more, asked even more questions. I've spoken with people all throughout the district, and just listening to their perspective, which is something that I said that I would always do, I would at least listen. From the beginning, I have articulated that this is not about baseball for me. I am not a baseball fan. It has nothing to do with baseball for me. It's about the community impact and opportunity. That's what this is for me. I have had extensive conversation with the Rays ownership, with our staff, with the administration about my expectations. We've spoken about the history of unfulfilled promises to communities when transformative projects and opportunities like this come about and the impact it has had on public trust. And I believe that they have listened and heard me. The Rays, the county, and the city have all come together and compromised. This deal is not perfect. I think we all could admit that. But what I do see is opportunity. I see opportunity for our youth, not just kindergarten through 12th grade, but our college students as well. I see opportunity for our youth sports and facilities, like the Belmont Heights Little League and the Yellow Jackets that are going to get that much-needed attention that they deserve. I see a creative approach to collaborate with our schools and our nonprofits. I see job opportunities for living wages for our youth, for our college students, for our Returning Citizens and an intentional approach to hire in areas such as Sulphur Springs and East Tampa, which I have articulated to the Rays' ownership. Quality careers, not just in concessions. I see opportunity for our small -- i'm going to Need Way more time, so put it on there. Put it on there. Put it on there.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Just kill the timer.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: I'm going to need time. I see opportunity for our small local women and minority owned businesses for contracts, prime and subcontracts. I see the opportunity for affordable housing at 80 and 60 percent AMI which I have extensively expressed to the Rays' ownership. Not just for the development, but throughout the city in areas such as East Tampa and Sulphur Springs, which I have also articulated to the Rays' ownership. I see the opportunity for the CRA extensions for East Tampa. Because that conversation is not over. Opportunities for transit, which we've -- we had that discussion today, F.D.O.T. Explained opportunities for transit. I see community input and accountability with the Community Benefits Advisory Committee to check that report card, to make sure that these community benefits are going to be delivered to the community, and that's why i've been supportive of this. Youth opportunities and investment, affordable housing, jobs with living wages, opportunities for small local women and minority owned businesses. All the things that I have asked for and have extensively expressed to the Rays need to be a part of this agreement and needs to go to the community. Lastly, there is a quote by a very famous woman, our forever first lady Michelle Obama, she says when they go low, we go high. I wanted to still applaud my fellow council members I don't think for one second that any of us took this lightly. And I believe we all did our necessary research and due diligence to come to the decisions that we have today. When they go low, when you go low, I will go high. And it's unfortunate that you took the opportunity as the only other woman on this council to approach Me The Way that you did, but I still will applaud you because as a council member, you do your due diligence. That's all I have. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I'm going to respond to that by saying my question is simply, you only support something --

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: You're not going to get an answer from me. I said what I said.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: That's fine, but I have a place to respond.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: You absolutely do. You can respond to yourself. I'm not responding to you.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: That's fine. You don't have to respond to me. But the issue is, you said i'll only support something with enforceable commitments and timelines. There are no enforceable commitments or timelines. The community benefit agreement could simply be nothing. You've said you've talked to them about it but there's no agreement made. They don't have to agree to anything -- i'm sorry. But after you sign this, after we sign this, they don't have to agree to anything. [ sounding gavel ] i'm sorry, you're not allowed to speak in public comment. I'm going to say --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I'll take care of this. Everybody in the audience, remember, you had your opportunity to speak during public comment. This is the council's opportunity to talk. Normally this exchange wouldn't happen. This is the biggest deal in the history of Hillsborough County and City Of Tampa. I'm going to let it run a little bit and let people get their points across. Councilwoman Hurtak.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: No. I mean, i'm sorry. I am simply repeating back what people said and i'm asking them to think about it. If you disagree, that's fine. But I have the right to ask the question. I wasn't rude about it. I haven't been mean about it. But i'm simply asking you if you think that's okay. You have umbrage with that and perfectly allowed to have umbrage with that. Doesn't change the fact that you said it and the fact that after we vote today, we cannot guarantee it. That's the ultimate thing.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Councilman Carlson followed by Councilman Viera.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I've had a bunch of people ask me, why did you change your mind? I didn't change my mind. The deal changed. All these conspiracy theories, oh, he must have bought you lunch or breakfast. I actually bought Ken Babby breakfast three times. I don't let anybody buy me coffee or breakfast so I can say no if I want to. I didn't take any campaign contributions from anybody related to the Rays. And the only thing that changed is i'm representing the people of the city and I want to get what is in the best interest of the city. Ken Babby reached out to me after the discussion we had a few weeks ago. I've only been involved in this three or four weeks. But when we met, I said there'S No Way you can convince me because you won't like what I say. He said what. Number one, no CIT. Everybody I talked to said no CIT. We took that off the table immediately. The second thing is I said we're essentially giving $180 million. I don't want to give $180 million. We took that off the table. So that went from $180 million to zero. And then they said, well, we still need money for whatever so we need a loan. I said, well, how about if we pay in four annual payments so we don't have to take out loans. Do pay go. Amendment 3 doesn't pass, we can pay go. Don't have to pay interest. The reality was the original deal, we were going to pay 180 million and get zero back. There's no chance of getting back. Everybody is saying, oh, what about the interest, got a guarantee or whatever, the reality is that now we will get paid back, small chance we won't, but before we had zero chance of getting paid back. And we'll get interest back. The next thing, and there's no new taxes. No new taxes for billionaires. We're not only not increasing taxes at the city, the county's deal, I don't know what the county's deal is we're not increasing taxes and we're not taking taxes away from anything else. The CIT is a different situation. Not using CIT anymore. Also, the original deal said the Rays wanted to control the Drew Park CRA. I talked to folks in Drew Park, and they said we don't want to be controlled by the Rays. We want to control our own future. So I said we need to set up a TIF because it protects Drew Park. It allows Drew Park to control ITs own future. And not only do they control their own future, keep the same base year so they don't have to start over again. Continue to get the money they had before and then we're extending the life of the Drew Park CRA. We're putting the future of Drew Park in Drew Park's hands. Not everybody in Drew Park wants gentrification. Not everybody wants development. This Way Drew Park controls ITs own future. Originally, there was going to be money to the Rays. Now, there's money to a Cdd, and it's not -- people can mention whatever conspiracy theory they want, Cdd is a very commonly used tool that's out there. The reason is that it is public, and it limits it to infrastructure. Originally, there were no CRA changes. Imagine if you were buying a car and the person trying to sell you on it, walk through the show room, hey, I want you to throw in the jacket or throw in the special wheels, that's what we did in the situation. Threw in extra things that weren't part of the deal, while in there, why not asked for it. Originally no CRA changes. Now extensions to East Tampa and some changes to West Tampa. Originally there was no money for roads or flooding. Now there's going to be a revenue source from the TIF and we're also taking half the Downtown CRA money that we can use on roads or flooding or whatever we decide to use. My proposal is roads and flooding because that is the number one thing I hear about. Please keep in mind section 19.7 Says that we are not endorsing the county deal. We are not approving the county deal. Our deal is separate. Fur against the county deal, go to county commission tomorrow. Our deal is a good one. Putting in an $80 million loan and access to three different revenue sources. Haven't talked about sales tax today. Not talking about bs economic impact numbers. The other thing, I want to promise West Tampa, Jamie Jones and the rest, i'm going to be there with you for the months and months and months helping you, whether anybody else does or not, whether the mpo or anybody else wants to go along, i'll be there helping you. I promise. I'm also not a baseball fan. Why would I vote? Because constituents want roads fixed and flooding fixed. When I get the e-mails, don't give money to billionaires, give it to roads and floods. That's exactly what we're doing. Access to three different revenue sources. Somebody mad about 80 million, please show up next week because we're talking about a hundred million dollars boondoggle stormwater project. Guess what, we have not seen a draft of the document. The document is not posted yet, and it will probably change right up until the moment and nobody is asking for a referendum on that. Please do, because that is a boondoggle. The last thing i'll say, some people say you're only doing this for legacy. Does anybody know, do any of my colleagues know, think about the biggest thing that maybe happened in Florida history and economic development was Disney. A picture of Walt Disney, Roy Disney and the governor of Florida. Was the governor? Hayden Burns. Nobody in the room knew who Hayden Burns. If you don't know who the governor was that brought Disney to Florida, what difference does it make for any of our legacy? In ten years, nobody will remember us. The only thing we'll be able to do is how this made our community better. We have to be happy with ourselves, not based on whether anybody else will remember us, even if your name goes on a building, eventually the building gets turned down. Remember any name, please remember Ken Hagan. [ laughter ] I just say thank you to the Community. Thank you to the Community for working on this. I hope we can come back together. Whatever happens, I hope we can come back together as a community. We're out there fighting every week on important issues. We hope this many people will show up. Hope people will be passionate and do research because we need your help every week. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Viera.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I appreciate it. Councilwoman Young spoke about some of her values. Things that I wanted to see in the community benefits agreement, I always tell them I defer to what Councilwoman Young said publicly on youth, empowerment, social welfare programs, Returning Citizens. We share those political values. We are bleeding heart type folks. I just wanted to commend you for that because I know that's always been very, very important. I'll say quick remarks, if I may. I talked about a lot of the good for the project. I'll be voting for it. Also bad. Economic projection numbers are just that, folks talk about amendment 3 and where that's going to go. The interest, tens of millions of dollars. Some significant money. There's gray but the good far outweighs the bad on this. I strongly submit. A couple of other things, we hear a lot about false choices, which is the idea if we turned this project away, boom, we're going to start spending money on fire stations and roads and all these different things. It's not going to necessarily happen. This is totally separate from that. Whenever it comes on issues involving public safety, I brought to the table and I was proud to do so, along with some of the skilled trade unions, Afl-Cio, but dealing with public safety, Tampa firefighters, Local 754, Hillsborough County Firefighters, Local 2294 and Tampa Police Benevolent Association. And I did that because I told the rays they need to be consulted. And if there are public safety challenges with that, you will not get my vote, along with other issues that I brought up. Ultimately, not only did these organizations whose sole purpose is advocate for public safety and their workers, not only not object to the project, they wound up supporting the project. Those who would say the project undermines public safety, I would ask, do you know better than the police benevolent association, than the firefighters? You do, that's like saying the Pope is an atheist. The folks, their sole purpose and life's purpose is earn 50, 60, 70, 80 thousand dollars a year to get shot at, to run into burning buildings. Die 10 to 12 years earlier than average folks because of everyday tasks and duties. To me, that meant a lot. There are so many projects that we can use the analysis on. Councilman Carlson talked about the south howard flooding project. By the way, I voted for. Other things, should have capped the Downtown CRA and taken that 25 million spent on the museum of art, for example, but i'm not going to put the museum of art against public safety, against roads, against things like that. I'm just not going to do that for many, many reasons. I remember talking to the rays when we first started meeting. I said you're going to be burdened by mistakes of the past and failure of the past. Mistakes in the past involving things like keeping up on public safety issues that I have very strong opinions on. Something that may not have any direct relevancy to the rays but certainly relevancy to the way people perceive this. They have engaged on that issue. Failures of the past with regard to Mass transit. Would like the penny sales tax 2018 all for transportation. Struck down in the Florida Supreme Court or 22 initiative by before we could vote on it got struck down in Circuit Court. Big issues. We should also recognize something big. Councilman Carlson talked about Ken Hagan. He is a republican. This is a bipartisan gesture by the county and city, Republicans and Democrats are coming together to do something big. Folks, that is a big thing, because that never happens anymore. It should. Maybe if you oppose this you go Republicans and Democrats are coming together to ruin our community. Whatever, right? To me, we're coming together to do a great thing. I'll say this as one of my final points, the courage of some of those county commissioners who put their careers on the line, right, in voting for a very, very big deal. People who will get opponents, maybe even other efforts, I won't get into because of their vote. I salute that. Harry Truman said I would rather be right than president. Some of these folks would rather be right than county commissioner. Potentially. Potentially. In closing, I respect the opinions of everyone up here on Tampa City Council. Everybody has stated their piece, and why they are voting yea or nay. Special deference on his legacy to Councilman Charlie Miranda. Above all of us just because it's a pleasure to serve with Councilman Miranda while he's wearing Black on this vote, no matter how much we may disagree. Thank you for that, sir.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: Sorry I missed the alternative I can't question. Claude Kirk was the governor in 67 right after Hayden Burns. He did come to Tampa --

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I thought you were going to get it.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: I was close. It was the next governor. I want to say we can disagree but still be respectful. I think we've lost that here. We've lost that in politics, lost it certainly on social media. It's interesting, but to explain what I mentioned earlier, my concerns with amendment three and all these other things, in 1996, with the CIT vote, the people voted on a community stadium. I believe that's what the wording was on the ballot language, and they had a voice. It passed at 53 percent, and Raymond James was built. So when the Bucs discussion comes up in a few months, whatever number they are going to ask for, I can at least say the people voted on it. It is a different contract from 30 years ago, it's different. In this case, with the CIT renewal, there was discussion at the county commission level about stadium and no stadium and no stadium. And here we are with money going not from us, the county is a separate deal, going to a stadium. If the CIT was renewed two years ago or said it could go to a stadium, I would have no issue because the people would have supported it. That passed 51%. That along with amendment 3, if amendment 3 wasn't on the ballot and I didn't have concerns what happens in November, I would have really no issue supporting something like this. I'm worried for what's going to happen because the financial hit is going to be huge if amendment 3 passes. So that's why i'm voting how i'm voting. I've been consistent since day one. It's not anti-anybody. It's not anti-rays. It's trying to be fiscally responsible. And that's it. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Miranda.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Thank you very much. Just a couple of things I should have spoke about earlier. What's happening to the tax assessor's building, Nancy Millan's building, on the corner of lois and MLK? I haven't heard anything about it yet. I don't know what's happening. Is that still part of this deal?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Any staff available to answer the question?

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Also the rehab building where the kids are at right behind the yankee stadium. Juvenile Justice. I just happen to know the answer as it relates to the tax collector and her lease. There is a lease that exists that goes through I think 2067, maybe 64, not really sure. I know that there have been conversations that occurred between the Counsel, the attorney representing the tax collector on that issue, Hillsborough College to ensure that that lease will be honored. So at this point, there's no plan and no understanding that that lease will not be honored and as an aside to that, if there is a decision to negotiate, they can negotiate that lease.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Is that part of the deal?

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: Not part of the deal, not an issue --

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: That building has 900 people a day from Middle Class that go there. 900 a day. The juvenile building, what's happening with that? Anybody know. Contiguous to each other. They make together a nice piece of property.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: I also have information on that. Happy to give you what I know. What I know is that for several years, been conversations between the Department of Juvenile Justice and Hillsborough County, facilities and real estate staff to identify other locations because they were seeking to move. Some of those went by the wayside and they actually, I think, had a site that they identified that there were some issues as it related to stormwater. I will tell you that the county had no knowledge of the most recent issue that came up relating to a decision to vacate early. We are working with them through a transition period right now. I actually spoke to the director of real estate and facilities this morning about this particular issue. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: The other one is the Downtown CRA, once that Downtown CRA is used, there will be no funds to put the streetcar heading north. That's my opinion. Furthermore that streetcar has to be expanded All The Way north somewhere. 54 miles of streetcars, now you've got about 12 blocks. But it is what it is. Put in by Dick Greco and Ron Rotella worked on it back in the greco administration. Cost $11 million for the whole thing. Now you can't do a mile for $11 million or a block for $11 million I should say. The next thing, what is a public facility? They say that a stadium or arena or whatever you want to call it is a public facility. I don't believe that is. A public facility is where you can walk into a library or something that a city park and do what you want. But they knew it would not pass if it was called a stadium or arena. So the geniuses got together, two words, public facility. And it passed by what Guido Maniscalco said 51-49. If they put stadiums and arena, it would have failed miserably. The public got fooled again when they put public facilities. I learned something today. Not today, I learned that the other day. And furthermore, when you look at police and fire, Mr. Viera, the first City Council that I served with wanted to do something for fire and police, and we got turned down by the mayor. And that was the only time that I can remember that the City Council overruled the mayor on a 5-4 -- I mean, a 4-3 vote. And furthermore, the next day we had a full-page ad, five people's names on it saying the firemen five and we never for there that. Thank you all for being here. I have no animosity to no one, not even myself.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you, Mr. Miranda. Councilwoman Hurtak, you pass. You don't have anything. No. Okay. I'll close this out. First, i'll start, streetcar. I don't think anybody here doubts my commitment to the Tampa streetcar and the proposed extension. I don't believe that this is detrimental. Having the CRA makes it a little more simple because we act as CRA Board without administrative oversight without the building -- but that money doesn't disappear. Money is still available, whatever piece that we need to have. It's just not necessarily dedicated to downtown. I will tell you if I felt like this was the end of the streetcar, I would feel differently about the proposal. I'm willing to entertain it because I think it's worthy of discussion. Honestly, we're making friends with people that have connections with tallahassee and i'm hoping those friends we've made will help us get our transportation needs met in the future. We're going to need a lot of help. Talk to Secretary Hall about this as well and you talked to folks, this is something that the entire community, we know we need. It's not just the streetcar. It is the connection between the airport and the downtown. It is the connection to USF. It's gaining access to CSX. Our transportation needs are great and we're going to have to find a solution that will probably have to be somebody biting the bullet and doing some kind of -- another all for transportation 3.0. That being said, i'll leave it at that. My support is not based on fandom like everybody says about baseball. You don't need to love baseball to understand the economic stakes. You do not have to believe every provision is perfect to recognize that this is the strongest agreement available to Tampa. Our responsibility is to not wait for a perfect proposal that does not -- that doesn't exist. Our responsibility is to negotiate the best agreement possible that protects the public and makes the decisions that best serves Tampa's future. That's what we've done. Tampa should demand more. We should demand more investment, more jobs, more housing, more walkable neighborhoods, more educational opportunities, more private capital and more economic opportunity. This agreement gives us a chance to pursue all of those goals while protecting taxpayers holding the private partner accountable. I've supported this project since the MOU because I believed in Tampa's potential. After months of scrutiny, months of scrutiny, negotiation and hard work, I am proud to support the final agreement because it is stronger. It's more disciplined, and better for Tampa than where we began. Reasonable people may disagree as we've said over and over about this project and respect those concerns. But I do believe that this agreement before us reflects serious negotiations, meaningful safeguards and substantial opportunity for our city. This is a vote to move Tampa forward. It's not only about building the stadium, it's about building Tampa. And that's why I will vote yes. Thank you. That concludes this portion of our program. We need to make a motion on resolution for 80. Who would like to make a motion to move that resolution?

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Before you take the motion, just for the purpose of the record if I could be heard briefly. Today, you were presented with an addendum --

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: We approved it this morning.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: And you approved the addendum. By so doing, you in effect substituted Friday's agreement for the one uploaded into Onbase. Mr. Steady and I have agreed that is the agreement, is that correct?

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Plus what you previously also agreed earlier today with the two proposed changes that were presented by the City Attorney that you accepted.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: I want to be clear. That is what you are voting on today.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: What about my additions?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: We didn't vote on that.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: I need direction from the council.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: That would be the sentence to add --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Actually, if you wanted to bring that to the floor, I would probably refer to Mr. Steady or Mr. Shelby about the legality of us, because that is something being negotiated by the county.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I talked to the county attorney about it and she said that was fine. Ms. Mandell said it was fine.

segments.speaker: Julia Mandell
segments.text: Julia Mandell, Hillsborough County attorney. Right now there are two blanks in there. Give me a second. Run with me on this. Two blanks in the agreement. There was a discussion among you to go ahead and just leave that number to the county. However, if there is a number that you are proposing, as long as the percentages remain, that's something you certainly have the opportunity to give to the county for their consideration.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I could see where this was legal if it wasn't binding if it was our suggestion.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: It's no less than.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I don't think we could legally bind the county --

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I talked to scott about this yesterday. He has the mayor's authority I think to approve our changes. If we make a change here, then it has -- the change has to get approved by the county.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Yeah, I don't see any harm with it.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Does that mean you vote yes --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Understand we can't bind the county.

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: We haven't bound the county yet. They have to approve all of this including the changes. What are we talking about? Community benefits agreement?

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Yes. The community benefits agreement to be no less than $75 million.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Second.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Obviously in theory I would have no problem with that. For Mr. Steady, if we pass this and then the county disagreed with the number and they sent something back to us that was distinct from what we sent them, do we have to revote on this?

segments.speaker: Scott Steady
segments.text: Yes. This is the sticking point. Unfortunately, this couldn't be negotiated because it is between two bodies. There was not -- we weren't going to all get together and --

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Inadvertent poison pill.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Mr. Shelby, can we negotiate on behalf of the administration from the dais?

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I'm not comfortable leaving a blank.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: You're voting no anyway. [ laughter ]

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: But if it's passing, I still have an obligation to my constituents to make sure there's something. Right now there is a big fat zero.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Mr. Shelby, can this council negotiate from the dais on this?

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: City Attorney told me yes.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Mr. Steady, go ahead.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: What if we pass this and then make that -- Either Way the county has to approve it. If there is a risk the county sends the whole thing back, why don't we pass as is and make a separate motion.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin

This is the first read of an ordinance in order to repeal section 14-111 and to amend 2-404 as well as amending 16-21 of the city ordinances. This is relating to a couple of changes that City Staff, legal is recommending based on potential preemption arguments relating to firearms. We are asking for these changes. I'm here to answer any questions.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Council have any questions? Hearing none, who would like to read this one? Councilman Viera, you are the public safety guy, do you want to read it?

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: I move an ordinance presented for first reading consideration. An ordinance of the City Of Tampa, Florida, relating to omitting any reference to firearms in deference to the preemption requirement of Florida statute 790.33, Making revisions to City Of Tampa code chapter 14, offenses, repealing section 14-111, chapter 2 administration, amending section 2-404, chapter 16, Parks and Recreation, amending section 16-21, of ordinances providing for severability, repealing all ordinances in conflict, providing an effective date.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Motion from Councilman Viera. Second from Councilman Maniscalco. All those in favor say aye. Opposed?

segments.speaker: The Clerk
segments.text: Motion carried unanimously with Hurtak absent at vote. Second reading and adoption held on September 17, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. In City Council chambers, 315 East Kennedy Boulevard, third floor, Tampa, Florida, 33602.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: The next one is something Councilwoman Hurtak wanted to call out. I'll wait for her to get back. Mr. Shelby, we're moving to you. Item 86, City Council rules. 85 was removed. We have 84, 86 and 41.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: It's been adopted. First reading.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Coming back on second reading. Thank you. Sorry about stepping out. You say you are here on number 86. Mr. Chairman.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Can I get a motion to move the resolution?

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: You have to read the title first.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: I move the resolution amending and restating the rules of procedure governing the meetings of the City Council of the City Of Tampa to primarily address public participation within the limited public forum created to conduct official public business, providing an effective date. We're doing Councilwoman Hurtak, 86.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I have a motion from Councilman Viera, second from Councilman Maniscalco. All those in favor aye. Opposed?

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Nay.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Just a clarifying question because I received some e-mails regarding number 86. Does this take away having public comment on workshop days?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Thank you for asking that question because I would like to clarify that for purposes of the public. One of the things that was suggested was that public comment on agenda items was limited to only 30 minutes. That's not council's direction. For as long as people want to talk about items on the agenda, council Will hear at the beginning of the meeting. With regard to -- your point was again -- the workshops.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: What happened with the workshops, the rule is now moved to a different section. Rather than being in rule 3 of meetings, it's been moved to be consistent with the rest of the public participation to rule 5. Now it states, again, there, that public comment will be limited to 30 minutes on the subjects limited only to the subjects of the workshop at the end of the meeting. That is what it states now. One more thing, Mr. Chairman, if you give me 15 seconds to update you. I took out the language related to the commendations for the union commendations. That really does not belong in the rules of procedure. That is between this council and the chair of the public safety as to how to conduct that. So I took that out entirely, and there's no reference to any distinction between union recognition and any other recognition that you have. It's a total of three items.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Administrative function.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Either a commendation or presentations, a limit of three for a 30 minute total in ITs entirety.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: But for clarification, there will be public comment allowed on workshop days, just for clarification.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: We're good? Let's call the vote again. All those in favor for 86, all in favor of moving the resolution, say aye. Opposed?

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Nay.

segments.speaker: The Clerk
segments.text: Motion carried with Hurtak voting no.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Very good. Item 41 is the last item we have to do -- i'm sorry. I forgot 84.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: We have I believe Mr. Knox here. Carl Brody from legal. At the June 25th meeting, we promised to come back with a proposal to move forward with the fee mitigation. I'm going to present it quickly, try to get through it as fast as we can. Two step process. First show why we need the change, and then we need to show the proportional -- proportionality of the new fee to the burden on the property. To get that done, the first thing we have to do is today, we have brian here, and he provided to you a memo on the reasons why we need this. That gets our first step done. We're going to present a proposed ordinance, this is proposed for City Council to review, if everything looks good, we can move that to first reading in September. After first reading, we can provide that ordinance to Revenue and Finance for them to do the actual study. And then about a month later, give them time to do the study, we can come back with a resolution and an ordinance, which would update the city code and also provide whatever determination of Revenue and Finance determines ben it does the study for mitigation fee. Those are the steps we're taking. Do you need anything from brian? If you don't, because he did provide a memo. That might be enough.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Yes. I guess my question was, you're going to show us an ordinance. Do we need to set it for September or do you already have it set?

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: I would like to you set it for September.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I move that we put this ordinance on the September 17 agenda.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Motion from Councilwoman Hurtak. A second from councilman Miranda. All in favor say aye. Opposed? Ayes have it.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Thank you so much for your work on this.

segments.speaker: Carl Brody
segments.text: All right. Very good.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Do I have it correct, item 41 is the last item of business, correct? Item 41. Emma Gregory, Legal Department. I am here in person, but I think Brandon Campbell, mobility director, is online. I think he's your first line of questions, but i'm also here for questions.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: So we heard in public comment today about Mr. Bhide being a part of this. And there were concerns that I think the new rule is that you can't be a -- participate in city business for SIX years. Two. Actually, they changed it to SIX. I'm sorry. That's Electeds. Apologies. So two years. Mr. Campbell.

segments.speaker: Brandon Campbell
segments.text: Yes, good evening, council. Can you hear me?

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Brandon Campbell
segments.text: Good evening, council. Brandon Campbell, mobility director. Item 41 on the consent agenda is an amendment to a previously executed agreement with the Tampa Bay Partnership for the Tampa Bay Regional Infrastructure Accelerator Coordination Services that they are providing. This is not related to the item that was brought in front of council during public comments. That document does not have a relationship with this. If there are questions about previous employees doing business with the city, I would defer to the Legal Department on that, but there's not a relationship between mr. Bhide and the item that is in front of you tonight.

segments.speaker: Emma Gregory
segments.text: I can't remember. Maybe it was earlier today or earlier this week, I spoke with one of my colleagues in the Legal Department because this employment question isn't typically what I address in my day-to-day practice. However, Ms. Hamilton's opinion regarding Mr. Bhide's work on a preexisting contract that is not this agreement, not what's in front of you -- he went to a huge engineering firm with like a hundred thousand employees that had existing contracts with the city. Work pursuant to those existing contracts, if he's even doing it, truthfully, I don't know, would be okay if it's filling preexisting work. If you have more questions about it, I can certainly follow up with my colleagues.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: That answers my question. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I had that line of questions. I object to having former employees who were involved in lawsuits and involved in leading projects in the city. I also object to the Tampa Bay Partnership being involved or running this in Any Way. First of all, it is an exclusive organization where you have to pay $50,000 and get approved by the Current or Former Mayor to be a member. And then also they have been involved in the last, all of the five ballot initiatives that lost, and they were involved in creating TBARTA which failed. So I don't see any reason to give them any activity that would involve transportation any more.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Any other questions of staff? Hearing no other questions, I have a motion to approve the resolution from Councilman Maniscalco. Second from Councilman Viera. All those in favor say aye. Opposed?

segments.speaker: The Clerk
segments.text: Motion carried with Carlson voting no.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. That concludes our agenda. We have new business. Councilman Carlson.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I have my form for 52 and 53 --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Motion to accept the form from Councilman Viera, second from Councilman Maniscalco. All those in favor aye. Opposed, ayes have it? Anything else?

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Two quick ones, if I may, you all may have seen that Tampa Bay Times report on children with autism having a significantly higher propensity on drowning in storm ponds, municipal local government ponds and so forth. I think the number is that it is one out of 25 kids that have autism and about 25% of drowning victims who are youth, folks with autism. So i'm doing a community meeting in late September here with Commissioner Harry Cohen on this. I would like to have, if I may, just a staff report based on the input we get from that community meeting on what the city can do in working with the county to prevent drowning deaths among children with autism -- or rather intellectual disabilities on that date. In person.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I have a motion from Councilman Maniscalco. -- sorry, Councilman Viera, second from Councilman Maniscalco. I am so tired. All those in favor, aye. Opposed? Ayes have it.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: I'm glad you brought that up because you see in the news how often it happens. It's horrifying. With my daughter, she loves the water. She loves the pool. That's where we have dead bolts because you read these stories and it's terrible. I'm glad you brought that up.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Everybody thinks it can't happen to them.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Yes, sir, and obviously Councilman Maniscalco, when I leave, I hope you run with that because you have such a personal connection as well as a great heart. My second one is for Mr. Shelby, this is my last one, we're all tired. I'm exhausted. We have our City of Tampa Veterans Advisory Board. Mr. Shelby, what is the process to have council members submit their proposed appointees for execution by this board?

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Is there a deadline attached to that, Sir? I think there was.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I submitted My Name.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Can you make that motion next week after you and I talk?

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Yes, sir. Sebastian will put that on. Thank you, council. Good meeting, Mr. Chair. And Madam Chair, thank you.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilwoman Young, any new business?

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: I move to make a motion to present a commendation on October 1, 2026, recognizing former Hillsborough County commissioner Les Miller as the honore of the first annual Robert Bob Samuels award of courage for the 2026 Black men's wellness day being held on October 10, 2026 at Al Lopez Park.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: We Love the Millers. Motion from Councilwoman Young. A second from Councilman Viera. All those in favor say aye. Opposed? Ayes have it.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Bob Samuels was one of the best guys I ever met. He started the National Prostate Cancer Coalition. I usually pass out halfway through lunch talking about it. Great guy with a great vision.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Anything else? Councilwoman Hurtak. Hold on.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Not to say anything in particular about the particular commendation and motion on October 1st, just so you know, your new rules are now in effect. Please take note now that you have three commendations -- actually two commendations and a Police Officer of the Month. In effect please be cognizant of the fact that when you review the calendar, when it fills up, because i'm going to ask council and we can have a discussion about this another time, that a motion to waive the rules is problematic with regard to consistency.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Yes. Since we've been talking about this, all of my commendations are ten minutes and below. I've already started and it hasn't even been in effect yet. I already started the practice.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Very good. Thank you so much. Councilman Maniscalco, any new business?

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Ready to build a basketball arena? Councilman Miranda.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: I would like to make a motion for mayor's Hispanic heritage committee come before council on Thursday, September 3 during presentation and commendation to present a brief invitation to the council for the annual Hispanic heritage celebration.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: This was brought to my attention and I approved it because it is a brief invitation.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Also --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I have a motion from Councilman Miranda. Second from Councilwoman Hurtak. All those in favor, aye. Opposed? Ayes have it.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: Make a motion to present off-site commendation to mayor's Hispanic heritage committee on Tuesday, September 29.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Motion from Councilman Miranda. Second from Councilwoman Hurtak. All in favor, aye. Opposed? I would like to make a motion to direct the Legal Department to monitor the Hillsborough County adoption of an ordinance regarding short-term rental regulations and provide an update on the November 5 under staff reports.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Motion from chair Clendenin. Second from council member Maniscalco. All in favor? Aye.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Councilwoman Hurtak.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I have a couple of actual motions and then something I need to say. I have a motion. I want to accept my form 8b for item 81.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Motion to accept the form from -- motion from Councilwoman Hurtak, second from Councilman Maniscalco. All in favor, aye. Opposed. Ayes have it.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I move to have staff present a six-month update on the tree-mendous program tree plantings to include the number and types of trees planted from October 1, 2026, to April 1, 2027, on April 15, 2027, under staff reports.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Motion from Councilwoman Hurtak. Second from councilman Miranda. All in favor, aye. Ayes have it.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Last motion, move to have staff provide a monthly written report on the tree-mendous tree program tree plantings for each month starting November 19, 2026, for the planting period of October 1, 2026, through October 30, 2026. Then repeat the monthly report until the in-person staff report on April 15, 2027. At that time, I will reevaluate the need for monthly reports.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you for the reevaluation. I appreciate that being added in there. Motion from Councilwoman Hurtak. A second from Councilman Maniscalco. All in favor aye. Opposed? Ayes have it.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I have big news. Big news. I will just tell you that the reason that, Councilman Viera, that I didn't get you my veteran nominee on August 12 is because that's the day that I was diagnosed with breast cancer. So I have been diagnosed with breast cancer. I have been poked, prodded, mri'd, pet scanned. On Monday I had surgery to put a cord in because I start chemotherapy on Monday. I will be going through a 12-week cycle, and hopefully after that I will be through by Thanksgiving. I will still have to have surgery, but it is something that I have been dealing with. I have been going through, and I will tell you all that having to be here for 12 hours today has been very painful for me. I've had -- i'm in a lot of pain right now. So I will just let you know that based on my blood count levels, I may have to be virtual, but I won't miss a meeting. I will be here. I just want my constituents to know that I fought for you today. I will continue to fight for you. Nothing changes for me. It just might change where I am.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you for bringing it to our attention. I knew something was up. I think I speak on behalf of everybody, our heart and our prayers are with you. We'll be with you All The Way.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Yes, I appreciate that. The only other thing, people will ask what they can do, I say whatever your particular religious belief, i'll take blessings, prayers, good thoughts, whatever you've got. We're going to get through it. I have a wonderful team. My doctor found this on July 31st. I start my first chemo on August 31st. It's been incredibly fast. I'm incredibly grateful for all the wonderful care I am receiving. I am not talking about where i'm getting my care. Not talking about anything more personal. I just wanted to get it out there because things will be different for a while, and i'm probably going to join Mr. Miranda and Councilman Clendenin in not having hair but I will have a wig.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Should I get a wig? [ laughter ]

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Or everyone can just shave their head. I don't think that will happen. I just wanted to make everyone aware of that because it's been a really heavy burden to carry privately. Now I won't have to carry it privately.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you for sharing. Something so many people in our lives face challenges every day. It will be challenging and tough. I'm sure you'll kick it and get through it and back to the feisty woman we know.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Back? [ laughter ]

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I'm assuming you're going to slow down through this process a little bit. Maybe a little bit. Mr. Shelby, did you have something to add.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Council, i'll bring it next week.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Motion to receive and file from Councilman Maniscalco. Second from Councilman Viera. All in favor, aye. Ayes have it. [ sounding gavel ] we are adjourned.
